signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What four questions structure the assessment of joint pain?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: (1) Articular or periarticular? (2) Inflammatory or mechanical? (3) What pattern (number of joints, symmetry, size, axial vs peripheral, migratory vs additive)? (4) Acute or chronic?

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: How do you distinguish articular from periarticular pain?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Articular = pain on all planes of movement with a deep, diffuse ache (± effusion); periarticular = point tenderness and pain on one specific movement (tendon / bursa / ligament).

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What features define INFLAMMATORY joint pain?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Early-morning stiffness >30–60 min, pain that eases with use, swelling / warmth / erythema, night pain, and systemic features (fatigue, fever).

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What features define MECHANICAL / degenerative joint pain?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Pain worse with use and through the day, brief stiffness (<30 min), relief with rest, and little or no warmth / systemic upset.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: How is arthritis classified by the number of joints involved?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Monoarthritis = 1 joint, oligoarthritis = 2–4 joints, polyarthritis = 5 or more joints.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What is the key rule for a single acute hot swollen joint?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Treat it as septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate the joint (Gram stain, culture, crystals), ideally before antibiotics, and do not delay.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Why can you not assume a hot joint is 'just gout'?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Because septic arthritis and crystal arthritis can coexist, and untreated sepsis destroys the joint within days — so a hot joint is always aspirated even if gout is likely.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which pattern of chronic arthritis suggests rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: A symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints (MCPs, PIPs, wrists) with prolonged early-morning stiffness — typically sparing the DIP joints.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which pattern suggests osteoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: DIP joints and weight-bearing joints (knees, hips), worse with use, with bony swelling (Heberden’s / Bouchard’s nodes) and short-lived stiffness.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which pattern suggests a seronegative spondyloarthropathy?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: An asymmetrical, large-joint or axial arthritis with enthesitis / dactylitis, often with psoriasis, uveitis, urethritis or IBD (psoriatic, reactive, axial or enteropathic).

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What is migratory arthritis and what causes it?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Arthritis that moves from joint to joint — causes include gonococcal arthritis, rheumatic fever, viral arthritis and Lyme disease.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which systemic clues point to a connective tissue disease (e.g. SLE)?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: A photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, Raynaud’s, serositis, alopecia, and multisystem involvement alongside the arthralgia.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What is the classic presentation of acute gout?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Sudden, severe pain in the 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), red, hot and exquisitely tender, often waking the patient at night; negatively birefringent urate crystals on aspiration.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: How do the crystals of gout and pseudogout differ under polarised light?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Gout = negatively birefringent, needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals; pseudogout = positively birefringent, rhomboid calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD) crystals.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which older-patient syndrome mimics inflammatory joint pain, with proximal girdle pain and a very high ESR?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Polymyalgia rheumatica — bilateral shoulder and pelvic-girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness in the over-50s, a markedly raised ESR / CRP, and a dramatic response to low-dose steroids; watch for coexisting giant cell arteritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which arthritis pattern with normal inflammatory markers suggests fibromyalgia?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Widespread pain with multiple tender points, fatigue and poor sleep, no synovitis and normal CRP / ESR — a clinical (exclusion) diagnosis.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which blood tests are first-line for undifferentiated joint pain?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF and anti-CCP, ANA (and HLA-B27 selectively), plus U&E / LFTs before starting drugs.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: What does joint aspiration tell you, and when is it mandatory?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: It gives Gram stain and culture (infection), crystals under polarised light (gout / pseudogout) and cell count — it is mandatory for any acute hot joint.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Which red flags accompanying joint pain suggest a serious cause?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Fever / systemic upset, a single hot swollen joint, weight loss / night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis), a rash / red eye / oral ulcers, or recent trauma (fracture).

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.front: Name the 'look – feel – move' components of a joint examination.
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.back: Look (swelling, erythema, deformity, muscle wasting), feel (warmth, effusion, tenderness, crepitus) and move (active then passive range, and function) — then screen other joints, skin, nails and eyes.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What is the overriding rule for an acute hot swollen joint?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: It is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — untreated it destroys the joint within days and carries real mortality, so the priority is a diagnostic joint aspiration.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What is the immediate management sequence for a suspected septic joint?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Aspirate the joint before antibiotics (Gram / culture / cell count / crystals), take blood cultures, start empirical IV antibiotics, and refer for surgical washout.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: List the differential diagnosis of an acute hot swollen joint.
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Septic arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis (trauma / anticoagulation / bleeding disorder), reactive arthritis, an acute flare of inflammatory arthritis, and trauma / fracture.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: Which organism most commonly causes septic arthritis?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Staphylococcus aureus — consider Neisseria gonorrhoeae in young, sexually active patients (migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash).

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: Why must a hot joint never be dismissed as 'just a gout flare'?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Because septic arthritis and crystal arthritis can coexist in the same joint — you can only diagnose gout after the aspirate has excluded infection.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What should you do with an acute hot PROSTHETIC joint?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Do not aspirate it at the bedside — refer to orthopaedics for aspiration in theatre (to avoid seeding the prosthesis).

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What synovial-fluid findings indicate SEPTIC arthritis?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Turbid / purulent fluid with a very high white cell count (often >50×10⁹/L, >90% neutrophils) and organisms on Gram stain / culture — but no cell count reliably excludes sepsis; culture is definitive.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: How do gout and pseudogout crystals appear under polarised light?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Gout = negatively birefringent, needle-shaped monosodium urate; pseudogout = positively birefringent, rhomboid calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD).

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: Which patients are at increased risk of septic arthritis?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Those with a prosthetic joint, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use, or a recent skin breach / joint injection.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: Why is the serum urate unreliable during an acute gout attack?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Urate is often normal or low during the attack (urate precipitates into the joint and acute inflammation is transiently uricosuric), so a normal level does not exclude gout — and a high level does not confirm it; crystals in the aspirate make the diagnosis.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What blood tests should accompany the joint aspirate?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Blood cultures, FBC, CRP / ESR, serum urate, U&E and coagulation (especially if haemarthrosis or anticoagulation is suspected).

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: How can you clinically distinguish septic arthritis from surrounding cellulitis?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: In septic arthritis the joint is held still and hurts on any movement; in cellulitis / bursitis the joint moves relatively freely and the swelling is outside the joint line.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What are the Kocher criteria used for?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: To distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in a child: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12 — more criteria met = higher probability of sepsis.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: A hot swollen foot in a diabetic with neuropathy but relatively little pain suggests what?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: A Charcot (neuropathic) joint — a non-infective destructive arthropathy that mimics infection; it is often less painful than it looks.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What causes a haemarthrosis presenting as an acute hot swollen joint?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Trauma (often with fat globules if there is an intra-articular fracture), anticoagulation, or a bleeding disorder such as haemophilia.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What is the definitive investigation that separates the causes of an acute hot joint?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) with Gram stain, culture, cell count and polarised-light crystal analysis of the synovial fluid.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: What is the empirical treatment of septic arthritis once aspirated?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: IV antibiotics per local policy (commonly flucloxacillin, adjusted for MRSA / gonococcal risk) plus surgical washout / drainage and orthopaedic input.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.front: Which arthritis follows a GI or genitourinary infection and can present acutely?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.back: Reactive arthritis — a sterile, often lower-limb oligoarthritis after Chlamydia or a dysenteric infection, sometimes with conjunctivitis and urethritis.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: What is monoarthritis and what is the first thing to establish?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Inflammation of a single joint; the first split is the tempo — acute (days) versus chronic (persisting >6 weeks) — because they carry different differentials.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: How should an ACUTE monoarthritis always be treated until proven otherwise?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: As septic arthritis — aspirate the joint before antibiotics (Gram, culture, cell count, crystals), take blood cultures, and start empirical IV antibiotics if infection is possible.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: List the causes of an ACUTE monoarthritis.
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Septic arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis (trauma / anticoagulation / haemophilia), reactive arthritis, and trauma / internal derangement.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Define chronic monoarthritis and give its differential.
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: A monoarthritis persisting >6 weeks: osteoarthritis, chronic infection (TB, fungal, Brucella), a monoarticular presentation of RA / spondyloarthropathy, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour, and avascular necrosis.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: What is the commonest cause of a CHRONIC monoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Osteoarthritis — a single large weight-bearing joint, worse with use, with bony swelling and characteristic X-ray changes.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Which chronic infections cause an indolent monoarthritis, and how are they diagnosed?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Tuberculosis (commonest), fungal and Brucella arthritis — diagnosed by synovial biopsy and prolonged culture, as routine aspirate culture is often negative.
A benign proliferative tumour of the synovium, classically a recurrent blood-stained (haemorrhagic) effusion of the knee in a young adult; diagnosed on MRI and synovial biopsy.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Which investigation is decisive for a chronic monoarthritis that remains undiagnosed after aspiration?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Synovial biopsy — for histology (PVNS, tumour) and TB / fungal culture; imaging alone often will not give the diagnosis.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Why must you aspirate even a chronic-looking monoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: To exclude infection (including TB) and crystals, and to sample fluid for cell count and culture — a ‘cold’ joint can still be septic or crystal-related.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Why does a normal serum urate not exclude gout in monoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Because urate is often normal or low during an acute attack; the diagnosis rests on urate crystals in the aspirate under polarised light, not the blood level.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Which joint pattern suggests haemochromatosis arthropathy?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: The 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints with hook-like osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis — though it usually affects more than one joint; check ferritin / transferrin saturation.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: What does avascular necrosis look like as a monoarthritis, and who gets it?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: A single joint (often hip / knee / shoulder) with pain and later collapse, in people with steroid use, alcohol excess, sickle cell or fracture; MRI shows early marrow oedema.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: A hot swollen foot in a diabetic with neuropathy but little pain suggests what (not sepsis)?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: A Charcot (neuropathic) joint — a destructive non-infective arthropathy that mimics a septic monoarthritis.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Which crystals are seen in gout versus pseudogout?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Gout = negatively birefringent, needle-shaped urate crystals; pseudogout = positively birefringent, rhomboid CPPD crystals.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Which red flags in a chronic monoarthritis point to malignancy?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Night pain, weight loss, a rapidly destructive joint on X-ray, or a soft-tissue mass — arrange MRI and biopsy for a possible bone / synovial tumour.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: What blood tests support the work-up of a monoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF and anti-CCP, ANA (and HLA-B27 selectively), plus ferritin / transferrin saturation if haemochromatosis is suspected.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: Can rheumatoid arthritis or a spondyloarthropathy present in a single joint?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Yes — both can begin as a monoarticular arthritis (e.g. a single knee) before evolving; look for the systemic clues and repeat the pattern assessment over time.

signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.front: How does the aspirate differ between the acute causes of monoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Monoarthritis.back: Septic = turbid, very high WCC, organisms; crystal = crystals on polarised light; haemarthrosis = frank blood (± fat globules with an intra-articular fracture). Crystals do not exclude sepsis — always send Gram stain and culture.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: How is polyarthritis defined and distinguished from oligoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Polyarthritis = ≥5 joints involved; oligoarthritis = 2–4 joints; a monoarthritis is a single joint. The number is the first classifying step.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: What four pattern axes are used to work up a polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Number of joints, symmetry (symmetrical vs asymmetrical), joint size (small vs large), and course over time (additive / migratory / intermittent).

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: How do you separate an inflammatory from a non-inflammatory polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Inflammatory = early-morning stiffness >30 min, joint swelling, raised CRP / ESR, better with use; non-inflammatory (osteoarthritis) = worse with use, minimal stiffness, normal inflammatory markers.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which conditions cause a SYMMETRICAL small-joint polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Rheumatoid arthritis, viral arthritis (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C), and systemic lupus / connective tissue disease.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which pattern suggests a seronegative spondyloarthropathy?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: An asymmetrical, large-joint arthritis, often with axial (spinal / sacroiliac) involvement, DIP joints, dactylitis, enthesitis and extra-articular clues (psoriasis, uveitis, IBD).

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: What does an ADDITIVE course suggest versus a MIGRATORY course?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Additive (joints accumulate and persist) → rheumatoid arthritis; migratory / flitting (moves joint to joint) → rheumatic fever, gonococcal arthritis, Lyme disease.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which antibody is most SPECIFIC for rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) — more specific than rheumatoid factor, which is also positive in many other conditions and in healthy people.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: What is the classic viral cause of an acute symmetrical polyarthritis, and its course?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Parvovirus B19 — an acute, symmetrical small-joint arthritis (often after a viral prodrome / contact with children) that is typically self-limiting with normal X-rays.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: How does the joint deformity of SLE differ from that of rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: SLE gives a non-erosive, reducible deformity (Jaccoud’s arthropathy); rheumatoid arthritis is erosive with fixed deformities on X-ray.
Recurrent, self-limiting attacks of arthritis and periarthritis with completely normal joints between episodes; a proportion progress to rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which features point to osteoarthritis as the cause of a polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Older patient, DIP (Heberden) and PIP (Bouchard) nodes and thumb-base (first CMC) involvement, bony swelling, worse with use, non-inflammatory markers.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: A spiking fever with a salmon-coloured rash, sore throat and very high ferritin plus polyarthritis suggests what?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Adult-onset Still’s disease — a systemic inflammatory disorder with quotidian fever, evanescent salmon rash, arthritis and markedly raised ferritin.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which polyarthritis follows a streptococcal sore throat, and what pattern does it take?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Rheumatic fever — a migratory large-joint polyarthritis (part of the Jones criteria), typically in a child weeks after a group A strep pharyngitis.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: In a patient with polyarthritis, what does ONE joint far more inflamed than the others suggest?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: A superimposed septic arthritis (or acute crystal flare) — aspirate that joint for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals; do not assume it is just the underlying disease.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which extra-articular clues should you actively look for in a polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Skin (psoriasis, malar or vasculitic rash, tophi, nail pitting), eyes (uveitis, dry eyes), mucosa (ulcers), systemic features (fever, weight loss, Raynaud’s) and a preceding infective trigger.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: What is the significance of X-ray erosions when assessing a polyarthritis?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Erosions indicate an erosive inflammatory arthritis — classically rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis; viral and lupus arthritis are typically non-erosive with normal or near-normal films.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Why is early rheumatoid arthritis a reason for urgent rheumatology referral?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: Because there is a ‘window of opportunity’ — early DMARD therapy with a treat-to-target approach can prevent the irreversible joint erosions and disability that develop if it is left untreated.

signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.front: Which initial blood tests best triage a polyarthritis by pattern?
signs__MSK__Polyarthritis.back: CRP / ESR (inflammatory or not), RF and anti-CCP (rheumatoid), ANA then ENA / complement (lupus / CTD), viral serology (parvovirus, hep B/C) and serum urate.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is the core clinical task when assessing back pain?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: To triage into mechanical (benign, ~90%), inflammatory, or ‘red-flag’ serious pathology — while actively screening for the emergencies (cauda equina, malignancy, infection, fracture, leaking AAA).

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: List the red-flag features that suggest a serious cause of back pain.
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Cauda equina features (saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel change), age >50 or <20, past cancer, weight loss, fever / IVDU / immunosuppression, night or thoracic pain, trauma / steroids / osteoporosis, and progressive neurology.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is the clinical cluster of cauda equina syndrome?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, bladder dysfunction (painless retention with overflow), faecal incontinence, and reduced anal sphincter tone on PR.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is the management of suspected cauda equina syndrome?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Emergency whole-spine MRI and urgent surgical decompression — delay causes permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction; also do a PR exam and check post-void residual volume.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: How do you distinguish INFLAMMATORY from MECHANICAL back pain?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Inflammatory: age <45, insidious, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise / worse with rest, night pain, good NSAID response. Mechanical: worse with movement, eased by rest, no prolonged inflammatory morning stiffness or systemic features.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Which condition causes inflammatory back pain in a young adult?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Axial spondyloarthropathy (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis) — investigate with MRI of the sacroiliac joints, HLA-B27 and inflammatory markers.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Which back-pain features specifically suggest malignancy / spinal metastasis?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Age >50, a past history of cancer, weight loss, thoracic pain, night pain unrelieved by rest, and progressive symptoms; breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid commonly metastasise to bone.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Which features point to spinal infection (discitis / vertebral osteomyelitis / epidural abscess)?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression / diabetes, a recent procedure or bacteraemia, night sweats and focal spinal tenderness; Staph aureus is the commonest organism.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Who is at risk of an osteoporotic vertebral fracture, and how does it present?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Older patients, long-term steroids, and those with osteoporosis; sudden pain after minimal or no trauma, focal tenderness and loss of height / kyphosis.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: How can a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm present as back pain?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Sudden severe back / abdominal pain with collapse (hypotension) and a pulsatile, expansile abdominal mass — always feel the abdomen and consider the aorta in an older patient.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is sciatica and how is it tested?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Radicular pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal pattern from lumbosacral nerve-root irritation (often a disc prolapse); reproduced / worsened by a positive straight-leg raise.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What are the motor and reflex signs of an L5 versus an S1 root lesion?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: L5: weak great-toe and foot dorsiflexion, numb dorsum of foot (can cause foot drop). S1: weak plantarflexion, reduced sensation of the sole, and an absent ankle jerk.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: When does simple mechanical back pain require imaging?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: It does not — in the absence of red flags, imaging is not indicated; advise the patient, give analgesia and encourage them to stay active, as most settles within 6–8 weeks.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Which blood tests are useful when a red flag is present in back pain?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: FBC, CRP / ESR (infection / inflammation), calcium and ALP and a myeloma screen (serum electrophoresis / free light chains), and PSA in men — alongside MRI.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Which visceral conditions can refer pain to the back?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: A leaking AAA and aortic dissection, acute pancreatitis, pyelonephritis / renal colic, and a posterior peptic ulcer — the pain is often unrelated to posture or spinal movement.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: Why is MRI the imaging of choice for serious back pathology?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: It best shows the spinal cord and cauda equina, discs, epidural space (abscess), and bone marrow (metastasis, infection, occult fracture) — far more than plain X-ray.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What distinguishes a single nerve-root lesion from cauda equina syndrome?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: A single root lesion gives unilateral dermatomal pain and a focal deficit; cauda equina is a red flag with bilateral signs, saddle anaesthesia and sphincter (bladder/bowel) dysfunction.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is the first-line management of uncomplicated mechanical back pain?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Reassurance and education, staying active (avoid bed rest), simple analgesia / NSAIDs, and physiotherapy if needed — not opioids or imaging.

signs__MSK__Back Pain.front: What is lumbar spinal stenosis and how does its 'neurogenic claudication' differ from vascular claudication?
signs__MSK__Back Pain.back: Narrowing of the spinal canal (usually degenerative, in older patients) causing bilateral leg pain / heaviness on walking. Unlike vascular claudication it is relieved by flexion (sitting / leaning forward) and worse on standing / extension, with preserved distal pulses.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Into mechanical (cervical spondylosis, muscular, whiplash — commonest), cervical radiculopathy (nerve root), cervical myelopathy (spinal cord — the can't-miss), and red-flag serious pathology (infection, malignancy, fracture, rheumatoid subluxation).

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What is cervical myelopathy and why is it the can't-miss diagnosis?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Compression of the cervical spinal cord (usually degenerative spondylosis) — it is easily missed, progressive, and needs urgent MRI and surgical decompression before irreversible cord damage occurs.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What are the clinical features of cervical myelopathy?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Clumsy hands (dropping things, difficulty with buttons), progressive gait disturbance / imbalance, Lhermitte's phenomenon, and upper-motor-neurone signs in the legs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, clonus) with a positive Hoffmann's sign.
An electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine and limbs on neck flexion — a sign of cervical cord pathology (myelopathy, also multiple sclerosis).

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: How do you distinguish a cervical radiculopathy from a myelopathy?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Radiculopathy = a single nerve root: dermatomal arm pain, lower-motor-neurone signs (lost reflex, focal weakness). Myelopathy = the cord: bilateral hand clumsiness, gait change and UMN signs in the legs.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: Why is the rheumatoid neck dangerous?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Atlanto-axial subluxation (erosion of the transverse ligament / odontoid) can compress the spinal cord — particularly during neck manipulation or intubation; always flag it before airway procedures.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: Which cervical root supplies the thumb and the brachioradialis reflex?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: C6 — sensory to the thumb and index finger, weak wrist extension, and the brachioradialis (supinator) jerk. (C5 = deltoid/biceps jerk; C7 = middle finger/triceps jerk.)

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What is whiplash and how is it managed?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: A mechanical neck injury from rapid flexion-extension (typically a rear-end collision), with delayed-onset pain and stiffness and no neurology; managed with reassurance, analgesia and early mobilisation — not a collar.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: Which features suggest neck pain is actually referred cardiac pain?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Exertional pain radiating to the jaw, neck or arm, relieved by rest, often with autonomic features — consider angina or acute coronary syndrome, not a musculoskeletal cause.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: How does carotid or vertebral artery dissection present with neck pain?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Neck (or face / head) pain with a partial Horner's syndrome (carotid) or posterior-circulation stroke (vertebral), often in a younger patient after trauma or neck manipulation; diagnose with CT / MR angiography.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: When febrile, what does a stiff neck mean and how does it differ from mechanical stiffness?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Meningism — neck stiffness with fever, photophobia and headache suggests meningitis; it resists passive neck flexion (with rotation relatively preserved), whereas mechanical spondylitic stiffness limits rotation and is not systemic.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What rule guides imaging after neck trauma?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: The Canadian C-spine rule — used to decide who needs cervical-spine imaging (CT); high-risk features (age, dangerous mechanism, paraesthesia) mandate imaging, and the neck is immobilised until cleared.
Neck extension with lateral flexion and axial loading toward the symptomatic side reproduces radicular arm pain — a bedside test supporting a cervical radiculopathy.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: When does mechanical neck pain require imaging?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: It does not in the absence of red flags — manage with analgesia, reassurance and staying mobile; reserve MRI for myelopathy / radiculopathy with deficit or red-flag features.

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What is Hoffmann's sign and what does it indicate?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Flicking the nail of the middle finger causes reflex flexion of the thumb and index finger — an upper-motor-neurone sign supporting cervical myelopathy (cord compression).

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: Which red flags in neck pain point to infection or malignancy?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Fever, IV drug use or immunosuppression (discitis / epidural abscess) and past cancer, weight loss or night pain (metastasis) — both warrant urgent MRI and appropriate bloods.

Age-related degeneration of the cervical discs and facet joints — the commonest cause of chronic mechanical neck pain, which can also narrow the canal (myelopathy) or the exit foramina (radiculopathy).

signs__MSK__Neck Pain.front: What is the first-line management of uncomplicated mechanical neck pain?
signs__MSK__Neck Pain.back: Reassurance, simple analgesia / NSAIDs, and encouraging normal movement (avoid a collar and prolonged rest); most settles within a few weeks.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What must be excluded before calling a complaint 'muscle weakness'?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: That it is true loss of power and not a mimic — pain-limited effort (arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica) or generalised fatigue / asthenia, in which formal power is actually normal.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: How do you localise true weakness to muscle, nerve, NMJ or central?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Myopathy: proximal, symmetric, no sensory loss, high CK. Neuropathy: distal, sensory signs, reduced reflexes. NMJ: fatigable, ocular/bulbar, normal CK. UMN/central: pyramidal pattern with upper-motor-neurone signs.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What is the characteristic pattern of a myopathy?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Symmetrical proximal weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, combing hair) with no sensory loss, reflexes preserved until late, and a raised creatine kinase (CK).

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: Which functional tasks specifically reveal proximal (myopathic) weakness?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Rising from a chair or squat, climbing stairs, and raising the arms above the head (combing hair / hanging washing) — distal weakness instead affects fine hand tasks and causes tripping.

Inflammatory myopathies causing symmetrical proximal weakness with a high CK; dermatomyositis additionally has skin signs (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules), whereas polymyositis has the weakness without the rash.
A heliotrope (violaceous) rash of the eyelids, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and the shawl / V sign (photosensitive erythema of the shoulders and upper chest) with nailfold capillary changes.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: Why is adult dermatomyositis important to recognise beyond the muscle disease?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: It is frequently paraneoplastic — associated with an underlying malignancy (e.g. ovarian, lung, GI); every adult with dermatomyositis needs a malignancy screen.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What is rhabdomyolysis and how does it present?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Acute skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin — muscle pain and weakness with dark (tea-coloured) urine and a markedly raised CK, complicated by acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What is the emergency management of rhabdomyolysis?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation to protect the kidneys, plus urgent U&E and ECG to detect and treat hyperkalaemia; monitor CK and renal function.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: How does a drug-induced (e.g. statin) myopathy present and resolve?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Proximal muscle pain and weakness with a raised CK on a causative drug (statins, steroids, alcohol) that typically improves on stopping the drug; rarely a statin triggers an immune-mediated necrotising myopathy.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: Which endocrine disorders cause a proximal myopathy?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Thyroid disease (hypo- and hyperthyroidism), Cushing's syndrome / steroid excess, and osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency) — so check TFTs, glucose/cortisol context and calcium/vitamin D.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: How does polymyalgia rheumatica differ from an inflammatory myopathy?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: PMR causes proximal shoulder/hip-girdle pain and stiffness (age >50, high ESR, dramatic steroid response) but power and CK are normal; an inflammatory myopathy causes true weakness with a high CK.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What defines a neuromuscular junction cause of weakness?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Fatigable weakness (worse with use / through the day) affecting ocular and bulbar muscles, with no sensory loss and a normal CK — classically myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR antibodies).

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What is a myasthenic crisis and why is it an emergency?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Severe fatigable weakness of the bulbar and respiratory muscles causing aspiration and ventilatory failure — it needs airway protection, FVC monitoring and ITU support, plus immunotherapy.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: Which investigations work up a suspected inflammatory myopathy?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: CK (markedly raised), autoantibodies (ANA, anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), EMG (myopathic units), and a muscle biopsy for the definitive diagnosis; plus a malignancy screen in dermatomyositis.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What does creatine kinase (CK) add in weakness, and how does it vary?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: CK reflects muscle damage — very high in inflammatory myositis and rhabdomyolysis (and in Duchenne / Becker dystrophy), mildly raised in many other dystrophies, and normal in NMJ disorders, steroid myopathy and pain-limited/PMR 'weakness'.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) and how does it differ from myasthenia gravis?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: A paraneoplastic NMJ disorder (antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels), usually with small-cell lung cancer; unlike myasthenia, the weakness (and reduced reflexes) improve with repeated use / exertion, and repetitive nerve stimulation shows an incremental response.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: How does Duchenne muscular dystrophy classically present?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: A young boy with proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, a positive Gowers' sign (climbing up the legs to stand), delayed motor milestones and a very high CK.

signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.front: Why examine swallow and respiratory function in severe myositis?
signs__MSK__Proximal Muscle Weakness (My.back: Because pharyngeal muscle involvement causes dysphagia and aspiration and respiratory muscle involvement causes ventilatory failure — monitor forced vital capacity (FVC) and protect the airway.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: What are the characteristic features of true bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: A deep, boring, unremitting ache, classically worse at night and not purely movement-related — unlike mechanical joint pain (worse on use) or muscle pain.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: What is the overriding concern with unexplained bone pain, and the key red flags?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Malignancy — red flags are night / rest pain, weight loss, a past history of cancer, and older age; these mandate screening for metastasis and myeloma.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which cancers most commonly metastasise to bone?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid — metastasis is the commonest bone malignancy in adults overall. Note that myeloma is the commonest malignancy arising primarily in bone (a marrow / plasma-cell cancer), as distinct from primary bone sarcomas such as osteosarcoma and Ewing’s.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: What is the CRAB tetrad of myeloma, and how does it present with bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Calcium high, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions (lytic) — an older adult with bone pain, hypercalcaemia, renal failure and anaemia; diagnosed with serum/urine electrophoresis and marrow.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which primary bone tumours affect young patients, and their hallmarks?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Osteosarcoma (adolescents, around the knee, 'sunburst' periosteal reaction) and Ewing's sarcoma ('onion-skin' reaction) — both cause night pain and a mass.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: How does osteomalacia cause bone pain and what are its biochemistry findings?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Defective bone mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency — diffuse bone pain with a proximal myopathy; low vitamin D, low calcium and phosphate, and a high ALP.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: What is the characteristic biochemistry of Paget's disease of bone?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: An isolated, markedly raised ALP with a normal calcium and phosphate; clinically bone pain, deformity (bowing), warmth over the bone, and sometimes deafness.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which biochemistry points to hyperparathyroidism as a cause of bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: A high calcium with bone pain ('stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans'), a raised or inappropriately normal PTH, and low phosphate; severe disease causes osteitis fibrosa cystica.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Why does osteoporosis usually NOT cause bone pain until a certain event?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Because uncomplicated osteoporosis is painless — pain arises only when it causes a fracture (e.g. vertebral crush fracture); bone pain should prompt a search for another cause.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: What features suggest osteomyelitis as a cause of bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Fever with focal bone pain and tenderness; Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and Salmonella is characteristic in sickle-cell disease.
A fracture through abnormal bone (metastasis, myeloma, Paget's, or osteoporosis) occurring with little or no trauma — a red flag that should prompt a search for the underlying disease.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which blood tests form the core work-up of bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP), PTH and vitamin D, FBC / ESR, PSA (men), and a myeloma screen (serum/urine electrophoresis, free light chains).

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: How do plain X-ray appearances help in bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: They show lytic lesions (myeloma, most metastases), sclerotic lesions (prostate metastases, Paget's), periosteal reaction (primary tumours) and fractures — guiding further imaging.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which imaging detects skeletal metastases beyond plain films?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: An isotope (radionuclide) bone scan surveys the whole skeleton for metastatic 'hot spots'; note that myeloma lesions are often bone-scan negative, so use a skeletal survey / MRI instead.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Why must a suspected primary bone tumour be biopsied at a specialist centre?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Because a poorly-placed biopsy tract can contaminate tissue planes and compromise later limb-salvage surgery — primary bone sarcomas are managed by specialist sarcoma teams.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which cause of bone pain classically responds dramatically to NSAIDs?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Osteoid osteoma — a small benign tumour causing night pain in young patients that is characteristically relieved by NSAIDs / aspirin.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: Which sickle-cell complications cause acute bone pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Vaso-occlusive bone infarction (painful crisis) and, less commonly, osteomyelitis (often Salmonella) — both present with severe bone pain.

signs__MSK__Bone Pain.front: How does the pattern of bone pain help distinguish it from joint or muscle pain?
signs__MSK__Bone Pain.back: Bone pain is deep, localised to the bone and often nocturnal, independent of movement; joint pain localises to the joint line and is use-related; muscle pain is diffuse and exertional.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What are the three broad mechanisms of a limp?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Pain (an antalgic gait), weakness (a Trendelenburg gait from weak hip abductors), and deformity / limb-length discrepancy — each is examined and worked up differently.
A painful gait with a shortened stance phase on the affected leg — the patient spends as little time as possible weight-bearing on the sore side.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What is a Trendelenburg gait and what does it indicate?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: When standing on the affected leg the pelvis drops to the OPPOSITE (unsupported) side because the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) are weak or the hip is diseased (e.g. Perthes, DDH, hip OA).

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What is the single diagnosis that must always be excluded in a child with a limp?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Septic arthritis — a joint infection that destroys the joint within days; a febrile child who will not weight-bear has it until proven otherwise.
Predictors of septic arthritis versus transient synovitis of the child's hip: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12 — the more criteria met, the higher the probability of sepsis.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: How does transient synovitis (irritable hip) present, and what is its status?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: A well, afebrile child (typically 3–10 years) who weight-bears with a limp after a recent viral illness, with normal/near-normal inflammatory markers; it is a diagnosis of exclusion after septic arthritis is ruled out.
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, typically in boys aged 4–8; insidious limp with hip/knee pain and reduced abduction and internal rotation; diagnosed on X-ray of both hips.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What is SUFE and who gets it?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis — the femoral head slips at the growth plate in an obese adolescent (10–16, often around the growth spurt); the leg lies externally rotated and shortened with loss of internal rotation.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: Why must you examine the hip in a child presenting with knee pain?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Because hip pathology (especially SUFE and Perthes) refers pain to the knee/thigh — missing the hip examination misses these diagnoses; 'knee pain in a child is a hip until proven otherwise'.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: Which X-ray view best demonstrates a SUFE?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: A frog-leg lateral view of both hips — the slip may be subtle on the AP film; Klein's line drawn along the femoral neck fails to intersect the epiphysis on the affected side.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: How does developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) present beyond the neonatal period?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: With a painless limp or waddling gait, asymmetric skin creases, limited hip abduction and apparent limb shortening; neonatal screening uses the Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres and ultrasound.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: Which features of a limp should raise suspicion of malignancy (e.g. leukaemia)?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Night pain, pallor, bruising / bleeding, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and systemic upset — check an FBC and blood film; acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can present as bone pain and limp.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What features suggest non-accidental injury in a limping child?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: An inconsistent or changing history, a mechanism that does not fit the injury, delayed presentation, and other bruises or fractures of different ages — escalate via safeguarding.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What is the initial investigation panel for a child with an acute limp and fever?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: FBC, CRP / ESR and blood cultures, plus X-ray of both hips (with a frog-leg lateral) and a hip ultrasound to detect an effusion; joint aspiration if septic arthritis is suspected.
Arthritis persisting >6 weeks in a child under 16 with no other cause — joint swelling, morning stiffness and limp; some subtypes carry a risk of chronic anterior uveitis needing eye screening.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: What are the common causes of a limp in an ADULT?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Osteoarthritis (hip/knee), fracture, lumbar radiculopathy / sciatica, peripheral vascular disease (claudication), foot pathology, and inflammatory arthritis.

signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.front: How is a confirmed SUFE managed, and what is the main complication?
signs__MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking.back: Non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral for surgical pinning (in-situ fixation); the main complication is avascular necrosis of the femoral head (also chondrolysis).

An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibia in a young child (roughly 1–3 years) after a minor twisting injury, presenting with a limp or refusal to weight-bear; it may be subtle or invisible on the initial X-ray.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What are the four textures of a swollen joint, felt at the bedside?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Effusion (fluid — fluctuant), synovial thickening (boggy / doughy), bony swelling (hard, osteophytes), and periarticular swelling (bursa, ganglion, tophus, cyst — beside the joint).

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How do you demonstrate a LARGE knee effusion?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: The patellar tap — empty the suprapatellar pouch with one hand, then push the patella sharply downward; a palpable 'tap' as it strikes the femur confirms a large effusion.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How do you detect a SMALL knee effusion?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: The bulge (wipe) test — stroke fluid out of the medial side of the joint, then stroke the lateral side and watch a fluid wave 'bulge' back medially.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What does a hot, red, tender joint effusion mean until proven otherwise?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Septic arthritis — it must be aspirated before antibiotics (Gram stain, culture, crystals, cell count), with blood cultures taken; crystals indicate gout/pseudogout instead.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What does a boggy, doughy joint swelling indicate?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Synovial thickening from inflammatory synovitis — typically a symmetrical small-joint (MCP/PIP/wrist) swelling of rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What does a hard, bony joint swelling indicate?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Osteoarthritis — osteophyte formation gives hard swelling with Heberden's nodes (DIP) and Bouchard's nodes (PIP), in an older, non-inflammatory pattern.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What are Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Bony swellings of osteoarthritis: Heberden's nodes at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and Bouchard's nodes at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How does a bursitis differ from a joint effusion on examination?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: A bursitis is a fluctuant swelling over the bursa (e.g. olecranon, prepatellar 'housemaid's knee') and the joint itself moves freely; an effusion distends the joint line and limits movement.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What is a Baker's cyst and why does it matter?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: A popliteal (behind-the-knee) synovial cyst, often secondary to knee OA/RA; if it ruptures it causes calf pain and swelling that mimics a DVT.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What causes a haemarthrosis presenting as a tense joint effusion?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Trauma (ligament rupture or intra-articular fracture), anticoagulation, or a bleeding disorder (haemophilia); a fat-fluid level (lipohaemarthrosis) indicates an intra-articular fracture.
A firm, cystic swelling arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath (commonly the dorsum of the wrist), containing gelatinous fluid; benign and often transilluminable.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: Which single investigation is most decisive for a significant or hot joint effusion?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) — sending synovial fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals distinguishes septic, crystal, haemorrhagic and inflammatory effusions.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How does ultrasound help assess joint swelling?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: It confirms an effusion or synovitis (and detects power-Doppler inflammatory activity), distinguishes fluid from solid swelling, and guides aspiration/injection.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How does X-ray help in the work-up of a swollen joint?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: It shows osteophytes and joint-space loss (OA), erosions (RA/psoriatic), chondrocalcinosis (pseudogout), and fractures — complementing the aspirate.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: How do you distinguish an articular (in-joint) from a periarticular (beside-joint) swelling?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: An articular swelling distends the whole joint line, is fluctuant/boggy and limits joint movement; a periarticular swelling (bursa, ganglion, tophus, cyst) is a discrete lump outside the joint with free joint movement.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: Which blood tests support the assessment of an inflammatory joint swelling?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: CRP / ESR (inflammation), serum urate (gout), and RF and anti-CCP (rheumatoid); plus blood cultures if septic arthritis is suspected.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: What is a gouty tophus and where is it found?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: A firm, chalky-white deposit of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints and soft tissues — classically the helix of the ear, first MTP joint and finger/toe joints in chronic gout.

signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.front: Which chronic joint swelling needs early rheumatology referral, and why?
signs__MSK__Joint Swelling.back: A boggy synovitis persisting beyond about 6 weeks (suspected rheumatoid arthritis) — there is a treat-to-target 'window of opportunity' to start DMARDs before irreversible erosions form.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What is the single most useful question when assessing joint stiffness?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Is it inflammatory or mechanical? — inflammatory stiffness is prolonged and eases with use; mechanical stiffness is brief and worsens with use.
Early-morning stiffness (EMS) lasting >30–60 minutes that eases with activity and is worse after rest — the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthropathy and polymyalgia rheumatica.
Brief 'gelling' (<30 minutes) after inactivity that quickly wears off, with stiffness and pain worse with use later in the day — the pattern of osteoarthritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What is the classic stiffness pattern of rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Symmetrical small-joint (MCP, PIP, wrist) early-morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, with boggy synovial swelling and systemic features.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: How does polymyalgia rheumatica present, and what is normal?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Proximal shoulder and hip-girdle pain and stiffness in a patient >50, with a high ESR and a dramatic steroid response — but muscle power is normal (it is stiffness/pain, not weakness).

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: Why must you screen for giant cell arteritis in a patient with PMR?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Because the two overlap; new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual loss indicates GCA — a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate high-dose steroids.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What inflammatory stiffness pattern suggests axial spondyloarthropathy?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Inflammatory back / buttock stiffness in a young adult that is worse with rest and better with exercise, with prolonged morning stiffness — e.g. ankylosing spondylitis.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What is a frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) and its hallmark sign?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: A painful, progressively stiff shoulder with global loss of both ACTIVE and PASSIVE movement, especially external rotation; strongly associated with diabetes.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: How does a frozen shoulder differ from a rotator cuff problem on examination?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: A frozen shoulder loses both active and passive range (a true capsular restriction); a rotator cuff lesion tends to limit active movement while passive range is preserved.
A joint that has become fused and rigid by advanced disease (e.g. the spine in ankylosing spondylitis, or an end-stage rheumatoid joint) — a fixed, permanent loss of movement.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What does a mechanically 'locked' joint indicate?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: A mechanical block to full movement (classically the knee that cannot fully extend) from a meniscal tear or a loose body — a structural, not inflammatory, cause.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: Which investigations are used for a suspected inflammatory arthritis presenting with stiffness?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: CRP / ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (RA), HLA-B27 selectively, and imaging of the hands or sacroiliac joints.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What is the expected steroid response in polymyalgia rheumatica?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: A dramatic, rapid improvement with low-dose steroids (e.g. prednisolone 15 mg) — a poor response should prompt you to reconsider the diagnosis.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: Why is prolonged inflammatory stiffness a reason for early rheumatology referral?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Because early DMARD therapy within the 'window of opportunity' can prevent the irreversible joint erosions and deformity of untreated inflammatory arthritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: How can osteoarthritis stiffness be distinguished from an inflammatory arthritis?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: OA gives brief gelling (<30 min) worse with use, in older patients, affecting large weight-bearing or DIP joints, with normal inflammatory markers; inflammatory arthritis gives prolonged EMS that eases with use and raised markers.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: Which stiffness pattern helps localise disease to the spine versus peripheral joints?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Inflammatory spinal stiffness (back/buttock, worse at night and with rest, better with exercise) points to axial spondyloarthropathy; symmetrical peripheral small-joint stiffness points to rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: What does 'gelling' mean in the context of joint stiffness?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: The brief stiffness of a joint after a period of inactivity (e.g. after sitting) that quickly eases once movement resumes — typical of osteoarthritis and lasting under 30 minutes, unlike prolonged inflammatory morning stiffness.

signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.front: Which two features together most strongly suggest an INFLAMMATORY cause of stiffness?
signs__MSK__Joint Stiffness.back: Prolonged early-morning stiffness (>30–60 minutes) combined with stiffness that improves with activity (rather than worsening) — usually with joint swelling and raised inflammatory markers.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What is the key first step when a joint has reduced range of movement?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Compare active versus passive movement: active limited but passive full = muscle/tendon/nerve problem; both active and passive limited = joint or capsular problem.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What does 'active movement limited but passive movement full' indicate?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A problem in the muscle, tendon or nerve — e.g. a rotator-cuff tear, a tendon rupture, or a nerve palsy — because the joint itself moves fully when moved passively.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What does loss of BOTH active and passive movement indicate?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A problem in the joint or its capsule — arthritis, a frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis), or bony ankylosis — a true restriction of the joint itself.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: List the main causes of a reduced range of joint movement.
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Pain / effusion (guarding), capsular contracture (frozen shoulder), ankylosis (fusion), a mechanical block (loose body/meniscus), tendon rupture or nerve palsy, and a fixed flexion deformity.
Hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint — a classic rheumatoid finger deformity.
Flexion of the PIP joint with hyperextension of the DIP joint (the PIP 'buttonholes' through the extensor hood) — a classic rheumatoid finger deformity.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What are the characteristic hand deformities of rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Ulnar deviation at the MCP joints with volar subluxation, swan-neck and boutonnière fingers, a Z-shaped thumb, and symmetrical soft-tissue (synovial) swelling.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What are the characteristic hand deformities of osteoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Heberden's nodes (DIP), Bouchard's nodes (PIP) and squaring of the thumb base (first carpometacarpal joint) — hard, bony swellings.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What is the difference between genu varum and genu valgum?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Genu varum = 'bow-legged' (knees apart; medial-compartment knee OA); genu valgum = 'knock-kneed' (knees together, ankles apart).
Lateral deviation of the great toe at the first MTP joint with a medial bony prominence (bunion) — a common forefoot deformity.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What is the difference between a contracture, ankylosis and subluxation?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Contracture = soft-tissue shortening fixing the joint (e.g. Dupuytren's); ankylosis = the joint is fused (fibrous/bony); subluxation = the joint surfaces are partially displaced (dislocation = completely).

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What is a fixed flexion deformity and how is hip FFD detected?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A joint that cannot be fully extended; a fixed flexion deformity of the hip is unmasked by the Thomas test (flexing the opposite hip flattens the lumbar lordosis and reveals the affected hip rising off the couch).

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: What is a mechanically 'locked' or 'blocked' joint?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A physical block to full movement (e.g. a knee that cannot fully extend) caused by a meniscal tear or an intra-articular loose body — a structural, not inflammatory, restriction.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: Which sudden loss of active movement suggests a tendon rupture, and how is Achilles tested?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A sudden loss after a 'pop'/injury; an Achilles rupture is tested with Simmonds' (calf-squeeze) test — squeezing the calf fails to plantarflex the foot if the tendon is ruptured.
A grossly deformed, swollen but relatively painless joint resulting from repeated unperceived trauma in a patient with peripheral neuropathy (e.g. diabetes) — a destructive arthropathy.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: Why must the neurovascular status be checked in an acute traumatic deformity?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: Because a dislocation or displaced fracture can compress or injure adjacent nerves and vessels; distal neurovascular compromise makes reduction urgent.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: How does X-ray help assess a deformed or stiff joint?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: It shows erosions and joint-space loss (RA/OA), subluxation and malalignment (varus/valgus), ankylosis/fusion, and fracture/dislocation — explaining the deformity.

signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.front: How can you tell a rotator-cuff tear from a frozen shoulder on movement testing?
signs__MSK__Reduced Range of Movement /.back: A rotator-cuff tear limits active abduction/elevation but passive range is preserved; a frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) restricts both active and passive movement, especially external rotation.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What are the two key tasks when assessing a soft-tissue lump?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: (1) Describe it systematically (site, size, shape, consistency, fluctuance, transillumination, mobility, relation to structures, skin, temperature, tenderness, regional nodes); (2) screen for the sarcoma red flags.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: List the red flags of a soft-tissue lump that mandate urgent sarcoma referral.
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Size >5 cm, deep to the fascia, rapidly growing / increasing in size, painful, or a recurrence after previous excision — refer on a 2-week-wait pathway to a sarcoma centre.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What is the correct pathway for a lump with sarcoma red flags?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Urgent (2-week-wait) referral to a specialist sarcoma centre for MRI and image-guided core biopsy — not local excision.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What is a 'whoops procedure' and why must it be avoided?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: An unplanned local excision of a lump that turns out to be a sarcoma — it contaminates tissue planes and compromises later limb-salvage surgery, so suspected sarcomas must be biopsied/excised only at a sarcoma centre.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What are the classic features of a lipoma?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A soft, lobulated, freely mobile subcutaneous lump with a positive 'slip sign' (edge slips under the palpating finger), usually painless and slow-growing.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What are the classic features of a sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A lump tethered to the skin with a central punctum, which may discharge keratinous material and can become infected.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What is a ganglion and its key examination feature?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A firm, cystic swelling arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath (classically the dorsum of the wrist) that transilluminates; benign, and typically firm/tense rather than soft.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: Where do rheumatoid nodules occur and in whom?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Firm subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces (classically the elbow / olecranon) in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What is the imaging modality of choice for a solid soft-tissue mass?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: MRI — it characterises the mass and its relation to structures; ultrasound is a useful first-line test to distinguish cystic from solid lumps.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: Which two features most reliably separate a benign lump from a sarcoma?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Size (>5 cm) and depth (deep to the deep fascia) — a deep lump larger than 5 cm, especially if growing, is a sarcoma until proven otherwise.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: How does an abscess present as a soft-tissue lump?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A hot, tender, fluctuant swelling, often with overlying erythema and fever — managed by incision and drainage (and antibiotics).
A sign of a lipoma — the edge of the soft, mobile lump slips out from under the examining finger when you press on it, reflecting its lobulated fatty nature.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: Why must the regional lymph nodes always be examined when assessing a lump?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Because the lump may itself be a lymph node, and because a soft-tissue malignancy can spread to regional nodes — nodal assessment is part of every lump examination.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: How can you tell whether a lump arises from muscle?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: Ask the patient to contract the underlying muscle: a lump within or deep to muscle becomes less mobile (or less prominent) on contraction, whereas a subcutaneous lump is unaffected.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What is a gouty tophus as a soft-tissue lump?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A firm, chalky-white deposit of monosodium urate crystals in the subcutaneous tissue around joints and the ear helix, seen in chronic tophaceous gout.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: How should a small, characteristic benign lump (e.g. a lipoma or ganglion) be managed?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: It can usually be diagnosed clinically (with ultrasound if needed) and managed conservatively / reassured; excision is optional (for symptoms or diagnostic doubt) once red flags are excluded.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: Which lump is pulsatile and compressible, and why does it matter?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A vascular lump (aneurysm or vascular malformation) — it must be recognised and not simply excised, as biopsy/excision risks major haemorrhage.

signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.front: What features suggest a lump is a peripheral nerve tumour (neurofibroma/schwannoma)?
signs__MSK__Soft Tissue Swelling / Lump.back: A lump that is mobile side-to-side but not along the nerve, often with Tinel's sign (tingling in the nerve distribution) on percussion.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What is Raynaud's phenomenon and its classic colour change?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries (triggered by cold/emotion) giving the tricolour change: white (ischaemic pallor) → blue (cyanosis) → red (reactive hyperaemia on rewarming).

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What is the single most important distinction to make in Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Primary (Raynaud's disease — benign, no underlying cause) versus secondary (Raynaud's phenomenon — a marker of an underlying disorder, especially a connective-tissue disease).

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What are the features of PRIMARY Raynaud's disease?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: A young woman (teens–20s), symmetrical attacks, often a family history, with no tissue damage, normal nailfold capillaries, a negative ANA and normal ESR — a benign diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: List the red flags that point to SECONDARY Raynaud's.
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Onset age >30–40 or male sex, asymmetric/severe attacks, digital ulcers/pitting scars/gangrene, abnormal nailfold capillaries, a positive ANA, and systemic features (sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, dysphagia, arthralgia).

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Which is the most important connective-tissue disease to find in secondary Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) — Raynaud's is often its first feature, years before the skin changes; also SLE, dermatomyositis, mixed connective tissue disease and Sjögren's.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What does CREST stand for in limited systemic sclerosis?
Which autoantibodies distinguish limited from diffuse systemic sclerosis?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Anti-centromere antibody → limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST); anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase) → diffuse systemic sclerosis.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What is the role of nailfold capillaroscopy in Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: It examines the nailfold capillaries: dilated, tortuous loops with capillary dropout indicate a scleroderma-spectrum (secondary) disease, whereas normal capillaries support primary Raynaud's.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Which drugs can cause or worsen Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Beta-blockers, ergotamine, sympathomimetics (decongestants), and bleomycin — always take a drug history and stop the culprit where possible.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What occupational exposure causes secondary Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Hand-transmitted vibration from vibrating tools ('vibration white finger' / hand-arm vibration syndrome) — often worse in the dominant/more-exposed hand.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What is critical digital ischaemia and how is it managed?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: A digit that stays white/dusky, painful and does not reperfuse, or develops ulceration/gangrene — an emergency needing urgent rheumatology/vascular referral and often an IV prostacyclin (iloprost) infusion.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What conservative measures are first-line for Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Keep warm (gloves, hand warmers), stop smoking, and avoid beta-blockers and other vasoconstrictors — before drug therapy.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: A calcium-channel blocker — nifedipine (a vasodilator); for severe secondary disease or digital ulcers, IV iloprost and treatment of the underlying cause are added.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Which blood tests are used to work up Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: ANA first; if positive, ENA including anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70; plus FBC and ESR, and cryoglobulins if a haematological cause is suspected.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: How does Raynaud's differ from acrocyanosis?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Raynaud's is episodic (triggered vasospasm with a colour sequence and pain); acrocyanosis is a persistent, painless bluish discolouration of the hands/feet without the tricolour change.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Why is Raynaud's often the earliest clue to systemic sclerosis?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Because digital vasospasm precedes the skin and organ involvement, sometimes by years — so new Raynaud's with any red flag warrants antibody testing and nailfold capillaroscopy.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Which non-CTD vascular and haematological causes produce secondary Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Vascular: thoracic outlet syndrome/cervical rib, atherosclerosis, Buerger's disease; haematological: cryoglobulinaemia, polycythaemia and cold agglutinins.

signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.front: Why should beta-blockers be avoided in Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Raynaud's Phenomenon.back: Because they cause peripheral vasoconstriction and can precipitate or worsen the vasospastic attacks; a vasodilator (nifedipine) is used instead.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which nail changes point to psoriatic arthritis?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Nail pitting and onycholysis (separation of the nail from the nail bed), often with DIP-joint arthritis and dactylitis and psoriatic skin plaques.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What do dilated nailfold capillaries with capillary dropout indicate?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: A scleroderma-spectrum disease — systemic sclerosis or dermatomyositis; seen on nailfold capillaroscopy and associated with secondary Raynaud's.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What do nailfold infarcts and splinter haemorrhages suggest in a rheumatic context?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: An active vasculitis (e.g. in rheumatoid arthritis or a systemic vasculitis) — splinter haemorrhages also occur in infective endocarditis.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Describe the skin plaques of psoriasis and where they occur.
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), the scalp, behind the ears, the umbilicus and the natal cleft — ask about hidden plaques in a patient with arthritis.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What is the malar rash of SLE and what does it spare?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: A butterfly-shaped erythematous rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds, often photosensitive.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What are the two hallmark skin signs of dermatomyositis?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: The heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the eyelids) and Gottron's papules (violaceous papules over the knuckles/MCP and PIP joints).

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Why must adult dermatomyositis prompt a malignancy screen?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Because it is frequently paraneoplastic — associated with an underlying cancer (e.g. ovarian, lung, GI) — so every adult with dermatomyositis is screened for malignancy.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which skin signs indicate systemic sclerosis?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Sclerodactyly (tight, shiny, tethered finger skin), telangiectasia, calcinosis, and digital pitting scars/ulcers, usually with Raynaud's phenomenon.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What does palpable purpura indicate, and where is it typically seen?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: A small-vessel vasculitis (e.g. IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schönlein) — non-blanching, raised purpuric lesions typically over the lower legs and buttocks.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What are rheumatoid nodules and where do they occur?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Firm subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces (classically the elbow/olecranon and finger extensors) in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What is a gouty tophus as a cutaneous sign?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: A firm, chalky-white subcutaneous deposit of urate crystals around joints and the ear helix, indicating chronic tophaceous gout.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What is erythema nodosum and which conditions cause it?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Tender, red, raised nodules typically over the shins (a panniculitis); causes include sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, streptococcal infection, TB, drugs and Behçet's.
