signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which skin signs are specific to reactive arthritis?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Keratoderma blennorrhagicum (pustular/hyperkeratotic soles) and circinate balanitis (a rash on the glans penis) — part of the reactive-arthritis (Reiter's) picture.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: What is livedo reticularis and which conditions is it associated with?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: A net-like, mottled purplish discolouration of the skin; associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, SLE and vasculitis.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which antibodies confirm the connective-tissue disease behind a skin sign?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: ANA then ENA — anti-dsDNA (SLE), anti-centromere/anti-Scl-70 (systemic sclerosis), anti-Jo-1 (myositis) — plus ANCA for vasculitis and anti-CCP/RF for RA.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which cutaneous findings signal an active, organ-threatening vasculitis?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Palpable purpura, nailfold infarcts, splinter haemorrhages and digital gangrene — they warrant urgent assessment for renal, pulmonary and neurological involvement, and immunosuppression.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: How does examining the nailfolds help in a patient with Raynaud's?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Abnormal nailfold capillaries (dilated, tortuous loops with dropout) point to a secondary cause (scleroderma-spectrum disease), whereas normal capillaries support primary Raynaud's.

signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.front: Which discoid and other cutaneous features support a diagnosis of SLE?
signs__MSK__Nail & Skin Changes in Rheum.back: Discoid lesions (scarring, scaly, hypopigmented plaques), photosensitivity, oral ulcers and non-scarring alopecia, alongside the malar rash.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: How is chronic widespread pain defined?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Pain present in multiple body regions — both sides, above and below the waist, and axial — for more than 3 months.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: What is the central diagnosis in chronic widespread pain?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Fibromyalgia — a disorder of amplified central pain processing ('nociplastic' pain), diagnosed clinically once organic mimics are excluded.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: What is the symptom cluster of fibromyalgia?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Widespread pain + profound fatigue + non-restorative (unrefreshing) sleep + cognitive slowing ('fibro-fog'), often with tension headaches, irritable bowel and low mood/anxiety.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: What is the defining feature of fibromyalgia on examination and blood tests?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: They are NORMAL — no synovitis, a normal examination, and normal inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) and routine bloods; investigations are done to exclude other causes, not to confirm fibromyalgia.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: What are 'tender points' and how do newer fibromyalgia criteria differ?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Classically defined tender points painful to light pressure; the newer (2010/2016) criteria instead use a widespread-pain index plus a symptom-severity score and no longer require a tender-point count.
Pain from altered/amplified central pain processing (central sensitisation) — distinct from nociceptive pain (tissue damage) and neuropathic pain (nerve injury); it underlies fibromyalgia.
Pain provoked by a normally non-painful stimulus (e.g. light touch) — a feature of central sensitisation seen in fibromyalgia.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Why is a raised CRP or ESR incompatible with a diagnosis of fibromyalgia?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Because fibromyalgia has no inflammation — a raised CRP/ESR points to an organic cause (inflammatory arthritis, PMR, infection or malignancy) that must be found instead.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which inflammatory rheumatic disease is a key mimic to exclude, and how?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Polymyalgia rheumatica — proximal girdle stiffness in a patient >50 with a high ESR and a dramatic steroid response; unlike fibromyalgia its markers are raised.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which endocrine and metabolic conditions mimic fibromyalgia, and what tests exclude them?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Hypothyroidism (check TFTs) and osteomalacia/vitamin D deficiency (check calcium and vitamin D) — both cause widespread aches and fatigue.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which red flags should prevent a diagnosis of fibromyalgia?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Weight loss, fever, night sweats, objective/focal signs (synovitis, weakness, rash) or raised inflammatory markers — these indicate organic disease needing investigation.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: What is the cornerstone of fibromyalgia management?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Non-pharmacological measures: education/reassurance, graded aerobic exercise (best evidence), CBT, sleep hygiene and treatment of mood.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which drugs are used in fibromyalgia, and which should be avoided?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin/gabapentin are used; opioids and NSAIDs should be avoided (ineffective, as there is no inflammation, and opioids risk harm).

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Why is fibromyalgia a diagnosis of exclusion rather than one confirmed by a test?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Because there is no diagnostic laboratory or imaging test; it is a clinical diagnosis made from the characteristic cluster with a normal exam and normal bloods, after excluding mimics.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which condition overlaps with fibromyalgia when fatigue dominates?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) — characterised by disabling fatigue and post-exertional malaise; it shares central-sensitisation features with fibromyalgia.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: How does fibromyalgia pain differ from inflammatory arthritis pain?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Fibromyalgia is diffuse, non-articular, with a normal joint exam and normal markers; inflammatory arthritis has synovitis (swelling), prolonged morning stiffness and raised CRP/ESR.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: How is depression relevant to chronic widespread pain?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: Low mood, anxiety and sleep disturbance frequently coexist with fibromyalgia (and can mimic or worsen it) — screening for and treating mood is part of management.

signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.front: Which baseline blood tests are appropriate in chronic widespread pain?
signs__MSK__Widespread Pain / Chronic Pa.back: FBC, CRP/ESR, TFTs, calcium and vitamin D, CK, and glucose (with ANA only if lupus features) — to exclude inflammatory, endocrine, metabolic and myopathic causes.

It has a marked female predominance and usually presents in middle age (around 30–50 years); it is often associated with poor sleep, psychological stress and prior physical or emotional trauma as perpetuating factors.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What is an enthesis, and what is enthesitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: An enthesis is the site where a tendon, ligament or joint capsule inserts into bone; enthesitis is inflammation there, felt as tenderness at the insertion point.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What are the classic sites of enthesitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: The Achilles tendon insertion and the plantar fascia (causing heel pain), the patellar tendon and the iliac crest — insertional sites where spondyloarthropathy inflames the enthesis.
A 'sausage digit' — diffuse swelling of an entire finger or toe (not just the joint line), combining synovitis, flexor tenosynovitis, enthesitis and soft-tissue oedema.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which disease group do enthesitis and dactylitis define?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: The seronegative spondyloarthropathies — psoriatic, reactive, ankylosing (axial) and enteropathic arthritis — they point AWAY from rheumatoid arthritis (a synovitis).

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: How do enthesitis/dactylitis help distinguish spondyloarthropathy from rheumatoid arthritis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: RA is a synovitis (joint-line swelling) WITHOUT enthesitis or dactylitis; the presence of enthesitis or a sausage digit indicates a spondyloarthropathy instead.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which associated features should you seek when you find enthesitis or dactylitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: The spondyloarthropathy 'family': psoriasis and nail changes, anterior uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory back pain, asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis, a preceding infection, family history and HLA-B27.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Why should heel pain (Achilles enthesitis / plantar fasciitis) in a young adult prompt further thought?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Because insertional heel pain is a common enthesitis that can be the presenting feature of a spondyloarthropathy — ask about back pain, psoriasis, eye and bowel symptoms.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What is the dangerous mimic of a dactylitic finger, and how is it recognised?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Infective flexor tenosynovitis — a surgical emergency — recognised by the four Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, finger held in flexion, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and pain on passive extension.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What are the four Kanavel signs?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: (1) Fusiform (sausage) swelling of the finger, (2) the finger held in slight flexion, (3) tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and (4) severe pain on passive extension — indicating infective flexor tenosynovitis.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which non-spondyloarthropathy conditions can cause dactylitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Gout (acute, with tophi/high urate), sickle-cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome in a young child), and, rarely, sarcoidosis and tuberculosis.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which skin and nail clues support psoriatic arthritis in a patient with dactylitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Psoriasis plaques (extensor surfaces, scalp), nail pitting and onycholysis, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint involvement.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: How does reactive arthritis present with dactylitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Dactylitis and an asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis a few weeks after a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, often with the classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'), plus enthesitis.
Ultrasound (with power Doppler showing increased vascularity at the enthesis) or MRI (showing bone-marrow oedema and soft-tissue inflammation).

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What X-ray change is characteristic of enthesitis in spondyloarthropathy?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: New-bone formation at the enthesis (periostitis, 'whiskering', enthesophytes) — in contrast to the pure bony erosions of rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which gene is strongly associated with the spondyloarthropathies?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: HLA-B27 — strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and, to a lesser extent, reactive and psoriatic arthritis and enteropathic arthritis.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: What is the first-line management of enthesitis and spondyloarthropathy-related dactylitis?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: NSAIDs and physiotherapy first; conventional DMARDs and biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17) for persistent or axial spondyloarthropathy.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Why does dactylitis produce uniform swelling of the whole digit rather than just the joint?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Because it involves several structures at once — synovitis of the joints, tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon sheath, enthesitis and soft-tissue oedema — swelling the entire digit.

signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.front: Which spondyloarthropathies are HLA-B27 associated and enthesitis-prone?
signs__MSK__Enthesitis & Dactylitis.back: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and enteropathic (IBD-associated) arthritis — the seronegative spondyloarthropathy group.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What are the clinical features of a fracture?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Pain, swelling, deformity and loss of function, with focal bony tenderness, abnormal mobility and crepitus on examination (crepitus and abnormal movement should not be deliberately elicited).

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: How is a fracture described systematically?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: By the bone and site (proximal/shaft/distal, intra- vs extra-articular), the pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick), the displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening), and whether it is open or closed.
A fracture where the bone or fracture haematoma communicates with a wound / the external environment — a surgical emergency because of the high risk of infection.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What is the emergency management of an open fracture?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Photograph and remove gross contamination, cover with a saline-soaked dressing, give IV antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis, provide analgesia, realign and splint the limb, and refer urgently to orthopaedics/plastics (Gustilo-Anderson classification).

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What must always be documented when assessing a fractured limb?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: The distal neurovascular status — pulses, capillary refill, sensation and motor function distal to the fracture — before and after any reduction or splinting.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What are the two earliest and most reliable signs of compartment syndrome?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Pain out of proportion to the injury and severe pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment — both appear before the vascular signs.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: Why is a 'pulseless' limb a late sign of compartment syndrome?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Because compartment pressures rise enough to cause muscle/nerve ischaemia well before they exceed arterial pressure; the classic late 'Ps' (pulseless, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold) are a late picture — do not wait for them.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What is the treatment of established compartment syndrome?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Urgent (emergency) fasciotomy to decompress the compartment — alongside removing tight casts/dressings, elevating to the level of the heart and giving oxygen/analgesia.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What is fat embolism syndrome and when does it occur?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: A syndrome after long-bone or pelvic fractures (typically 24–72 hours later) of respiratory distress/hypoxia, a petechial rash and neurological signs (confusion); management is supportive.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: Which fractures can cause significant haemorrhage and shock?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Femoral shaft fractures (around 1–1.5 L blood loss) and pelvic fractures (which can bleed massively) — resuscitate and control bleeding as part of the primary survey.
A fracture caused by low-energy trauma (e.g. a fall from standing height) that would not normally break bone — a marker of osteoporosis; assess and treat bone health.
A fracture through abnormal bone (e.g. a metastasis, myeloma, Paget's or a bone cyst) occurring with minimal or no trauma — investigate for the underlying cause.
A fracture from repetitive submaximal loading (e.g. in runners/military recruits), often not visible on the initial X-ray — diagnosed on MRI or a bone scan.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What fracture patterns are specific to children?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Greenstick fractures (incomplete, the bone bends and cracks on one side) and Salter-Harris fractures (involving the growth plate/physis) — because children's bones are more plastic.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: Which features of a paediatric fracture should raise concern about non-accidental injury?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: An inconsistent or changing history, a mechanism that does not fit, delayed presentation, and fractures of different ages or in unusual sites — escalate via safeguarding.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What is the first priority in a patient with major trauma and a fracture?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: The ATLS primary survey (ABCDE with C-spine control) and control of catastrophic haemorrhage — 'life before limb'; the fracture is addressed after the patient is stabilised.

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What is the standard imaging for a suspected fracture?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: A plain radiograph in two views (AP and lateral), including the joint above and below; CT is used for complex or intra-articular fractures. A normal X-ray does not exclude a fracture (e.g. scaphoid).

signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.front: What are the general principles of fracture management?
signs__MSK__Fractures & Trauma (Clinical.back: Reduce (restore alignment), hold (splint, cast or internal/external fixation) and rehabilitate — with analgesia, VTE prophylaxis and treatment of any open wound or complication.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What is Tinel's sign and how is it elicited?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Lightly percussing over a peripheral nerve reproduces tingling / paraesthesiae shooting distally into that nerve's sensory distribution; it is positive when the tapping recreates the patient's symptoms.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What does a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist indicate?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Carpal tunnel syndrome — median-nerve irritation under the flexor retinaculum, producing tingling in the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger (radial 3½ digits).

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Which nerve and territory does Tinel's sign test at the wrist?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: The median nerve — its sensory territory is the palmar radial 3½ digits (thumb, index, middle, radial half of the ring finger).

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Where is Tinel's sign elicited for ulnar nerve entrapment, and what is the territory?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: At the elbow (cubital tunnel) — tingling radiates into the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Where is Tinel's sign elicited for tarsal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Over the posterior tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus — producing tingling in the sole of the foot.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: How sensitive and specific is Tinel's sign for carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: It is fairly specific but relatively insensitive — so a negative Tinel's sign does not exclude carpal tunnel syndrome.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Which test is used alongside Tinel's sign for carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Phalen's test (sustained wrist flexion reproducing paraesthesiae) — the two are complementary provocation tests.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What does an 'advancing' Tinel's sign along a nerve after repair indicate?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Axonal regeneration — the point of maximal tingling advances distally along the nerve as the regenerating axons grow, tracking recovery.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What is the anatomical basis of carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Compression of the median nerve as it passes under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist, within the confined carpal tunnel.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What are the classic symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Nocturnal tingling and pain in the radial 3½ digits, relieved by shaking the hand ('flick sign'); later thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Which systemic conditions predispose to carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, acromegaly and repetitive wrist use.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: What is the confirmatory investigation for carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Nerve conduction studies — showing slowed median-nerve conduction across the wrist; the clinical tests (Tinel's/Phalen's) support but do not confirm.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: Which muscles are weak and wasted in advanced carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: The thenar muscles (median-innervated: abductor pollicis brevis) — giving weak thumb abduction and thenar-eminence wasting.

signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.front: How is carpal tunnel syndrome managed?
signs__MSK__Tinel's Sign.back: Wrist splinting (especially at night), corticosteroid injection, and treating any underlying cause; surgical carpal tunnel decompression (flexor retinaculum release) for severe or refractory cases.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What is Phalen's test and how is it performed?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: The patient holds both wrists in full flexion (backs of the hands pressed together, elbows out) for about 60 seconds; it is positive when this reproduces tingling / paraesthesiae in the median-nerve territory.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What does a positive Phalen's test indicate?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Carpal tunnel syndrome — median-nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum, giving tingling in the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger (radial 3½ digits).

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What is the physiological basis of Phalen's test?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Sustained wrist flexion raises the pressure inside the carpal tunnel, compressing the already-irritable median nerve and provoking its symptoms.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: Which digits should tingle in a positive Phalen's test, and which is spared?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: The thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger tingle; the little finger is spared (little-finger symptoms suggest the ulnar nerve instead).

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: How does Phalen's test compare with Tinel's sign for sensitivity?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Phalen's test is generally the more sensitive of the two provocation tests, but neither is definitive and both can be falsely negative.
An alternative provocation manoeuvre using sustained wrist extension (rather than flexion) to reproduce median-nerve paraesthesiae in carpal tunnel syndrome.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What does earlier onset of tingling during Phalen's test suggest?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: More severe median-nerve compression — the shorter the time to reproduce symptoms, the more advanced the carpal tunnel syndrome tends to be.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: Which provocation test complements Phalen's test in carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Tinel's sign (percussing the median nerve at the wrist to provoke distal tingling) — the two are complementary.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What is the confirmatory investigation for carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Nerve conduction studies — showing slowed median-nerve conduction across the wrist; provocation tests (Phalen's/Tinel's) support but do not confirm.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: What are the classic symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Nocturnal tingling and pain in the radial 3½ digits, relieved by shaking the hand ('flick sign'); later thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: Which systemic conditions predispose to carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, acromegaly and repetitive wrist use.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: Which muscles are weak and wasted in advanced carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: The thenar muscles (median-innervated: abductor pollicis brevis) — giving weak thumb abduction and thenar-eminence wasting.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: How is carpal tunnel syndrome managed?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: Wrist splinting (especially at night), corticosteroid injection, and treating any underlying cause; surgical decompression (flexor retinaculum release) for severe or refractory cases.

signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.front: Does a negative Phalen's test exclude carpal tunnel syndrome?
signs__MSK__Phalen's Test.back: No — Phalen's test is sensitive but not perfect, so a negative result does not exclude carpal tunnel syndrome; rely on the whole picture and nerve conduction studies where needed.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: What is Froment's sign and how is it elicited?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Ask the patient to grip a sheet of paper between the thumb and the side of the index finger and hold on as you pull it away; it is positive when the thumb interphalangeal (IP) joint flexes to grip instead of staying flat.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: What does a positive Froment's sign indicate?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Ulnar-nerve palsy — weakness of adductor pollicis, an ulnar-innervated thumb muscle.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Which muscle is being tested in Froment's sign, and what is its nerve supply?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Adductor pollicis — supplied by the ulnar nerve (deep branch).

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Which muscle compensates to produce a positive Froment's sign?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Flexor pollicis longus (supplied by the median nerve / anterior interosseous nerve) — it flexes the thumb IP joint to grip when adductor pollicis is weak.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: What is Jeanne's sign and how does it relate to Froment's sign?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Hyperextension of the thumb metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint during the same pinch-grip test — a compensatory sign that often accompanies a positive Froment's sign in ulnar-nerve palsy.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: At which two sites is the ulnar nerve most commonly entrapped?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: The elbow (cubital tunnel) — the commonest — and the wrist (Guyon's canal).

A higher (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a LESS clawed hand than a distal (wrist) lesion, because the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is also paralysed, reducing flexion of the ring and little fingers.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: What is the sensory territory of the ulnar nerve in the hand?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: The little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger (palmar and dorsal), and the ulnar border of the hand.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Which hand deformity develops in an ulnar-nerve palsy?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: The ulnar claw hand — hyperextension at the MCP joints with flexion of the IP joints of the ring and little fingers (from weakness of the medial two lumbricals and interossei).

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Which small muscles of the hand are weak in an ulnar-nerve lesion?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Most of the intrinsic hand muscles — the interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar muscles and adductor pollicis (giving weak finger abduction/adduction and thumb adduction).

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Which activity classically causes ulnar-nerve compression at Guyon's canal?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Prolonged cycling ('handlebar palsy'), and other causes of pressure at the wrist such as a ganglion or repetitive trauma.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: How is an ulnar-nerve lesion confirmed and localised?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Nerve conduction studies / EMG — confirming the lesion and localising it to the elbow or wrist; imaging (e.g. elbow X-ray, ultrasound/MRI) looks for a structural cause.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: How is cubital tunnel syndrome managed?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Activity/posture modification and avoiding sustained elbow flexion, with a night splint; surgical decompression or ulnar-nerve transposition for severe or progressive cases.

signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.front: Why does the thumb IP joint flex in a positive Froment's sign?
signs__MSK__Froment's Sign.back: Because the weak adductor pollicis cannot provide thumb adduction, so the patient recruits flexor pollicis longus to pinch, which flexes the IP joint.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: First split intrinsic (moving the shoulder reproduces the pain) from referred (shoulder exam normal — pain from the neck, heart, diaphragm or lung apex). Within intrinsic, use active vs passive movement and the painful arc.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What do the active-vs-passive movement patterns mean at the shoulder?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Rotator cuff problem = active movement lost/weak, passive range preserved. Capsular problem (frozen shoulder or glenohumeral OA) = both active and passive lost, with external rotation worst.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What does a painful arc of 60–120° indicate?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Subacromial pathology — rotator cuff tendinopathy / impingement (± subacromial bursitis).

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What does a high painful arc >160° indicate?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Acromioclavicular joint pathology — supported by focal ACJ tenderness and a positive scarf test.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: Which rotator-cuff muscle does each test isolate: empty-can, resisted external rotation, lift-off?
What does a positive drop-arm test mean?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: A full-thickness rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus): the patient cannot hold the arm abducted and it drops, with weak active abduction but preserved passive range.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What are the key features of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Global loss of both active and passive movement, external rotation worst; classically diabetic; self-limiting through freezing → frozen → thawing phases over months; X-ray normal.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What shoulder-pain pattern suggests referred cardiac pain?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Exertional pain in the left shoulder / arm that eases with rest, with a normal shoulder exam → think angina / ACS — do an ECG + troponin.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What is Kehr’s sign and why does it matter?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Tip-of-shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation (referred via C3–5). With abdominal pain or shock it signals a ruptured spleen or ruptured ectopic pregnancy — a surgical / gynae emergency.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: What is the triad of a Pancoast (apical lung) tumour?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Shoulder pain + Horner’s syndrome + wasting of the small hand muscles (T1 root), often with weight loss in a smoker → CXR / CT chest.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: How does a septic shoulder present and what is the immediate action?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Hot, red, swollen shoulder in a systemically unwell patient who refuses all movement → joint aspiration (Gram / culture) before antibiotics.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: Which imaging confirms a suspected rotator cuff tear?
When is plain X-ray the right shoulder investigation?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: For glenohumeral OA, ACJ disease, calcific tendinitis, and after trauma to exclude fracture / dislocation.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: Do most cases of impingement / cuff tendinopathy / frozen shoulder need imaging?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: No — they are largely clinical diagnoses managed conservatively. Image when a tear is suspected, trauma has occurred, or red flags are present.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: Who gets glenohumeral instability and which test is positive?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Typically young patients / athletes with recurrent subluxation or dislocation; the apprehension test (and relocation) is positive.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: How do you distinguish frozen shoulder from glenohumeral OA?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: Both restrict active and passive movement (ER worst). Frozen shoulder has a normal X-ray; GH OA shows joint-space loss, osteophytes on X-ray.

signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.front: Before diagnosing a local shoulder cause, what must you always screen?
signs__MSK__Shoulder Pain.back: The neck (cervical radiculopathy), the chest (cardiac, apical lung / Pancoast) and the abdomen (diaphragmatic / Kehr’s) — the shoulder is a classic site of referred serious disease.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: Where is true hip-joint pain felt, and where does it radiate?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: In the groin, often radiating to the knee. (Lateral pain = greater trochanteric pain syndrome; buttock / posterior pain = referred from the lumbar spine or SIJ.)

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: What is the earliest sign of hip-joint disease on examination?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Loss of internal rotation (with the hip flexed) — it is affected before other movements in OA and other intra-articular disease.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: How is hip pain localised by site?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Groin = true hip joint (OA, AVN, fracture, septic); lateral (over greater trochanter) = gluteal tendinopathy / trochanteric bursitis; buttock / posterior = referred lumbar spine / SIJ or vascular.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: Why must a child’s knee pain never be dismissed?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Hip pathology in children classically refers to the knee — a limp or knee pain may be septic hip, Perthes or SUFE. Always examine the hip.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: What are the features of SUFE and how is it managed initially?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis: adolescent (10–16y), often obese, groin / knee pain, leg externally rotated and shortened. Keep non-weight-bearing, get a frog-leg lateral X-ray, urgent surgical fixation.
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children (~4–8y), causing an insidious limp with restricted abduction / internal rotation. Diagnosed on X-ray ± MRI.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: How do you distinguish transient synovitis from a septic hip?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Transient synovitis: well child, recent viral illness, mild limp, settles. Septic arthritis: febrile, systemically unwell, refuses to weight-bear. Use the Kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR/CRP ↑, WCC ↑) and aspirate if in doubt.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: What is the classic sign of a neck-of-femur fracture?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: In an elderly patient after a fall: a shortened and externally rotated leg, unable to weight-bear → X-ray (AP + lateral); MRI if the X-ray is normal but suspicion remains (occult fracture).

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: Which risk factors and imaging define avascular necrosis of the hip?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Risk factors: steroids, alcohol, SLE, sickle cell, trauma. Groin pain with a normal early X-ray — MRI is the investigation of choice.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: What is greater trochanteric pain syndrome?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Lateral hip pain from gluteal tendinopathy / trochanteric bursitis: tender over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side; a clinical diagnosis managed conservatively.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: Which special tests are used in the hip exam and what do they assess?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Trendelenburg (hip abductor function), Thomas test (fixed-flexion deformity), FABER / Patrick’s (hip / SIJ), FADIR (femoroacetabular impingement / labral).

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: What is the immediate management of a suspected septic hip?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Aspirate the joint (Gram stain / culture) before antibiotics, send FBC / CRP / blood cultures, then antibiotics + surgical washout. Applies to native and prosthetic joints.

signs__MSK__Hip Pain.front: Which hip diagnoses can have a normal early X-ray?
signs__MSK__Hip Pain.back: Avascular necrosis and an occult neck-of-femur fracture — if suspicion is high, proceed to MRI.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What are the two triage questions for knee pain?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: (1) Was there trauma? → ligament / meniscus / fracture. (2) Is the knee hot? — an atraumatic hot swollen knee is septic or crystal arthritis until proven otherwise. Then localise by site and age.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What does the speed of a post-traumatic effusion tell you?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: A rapid, tense effusion within hours = haemarthrosis (ACL rupture or fracture). A slower effusion over ~24h suggests a meniscal tear.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: Which examination finding indicates an extensor-mechanism rupture?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Inability to perform a straight-leg raise (or to extend the knee against gravity) after injury — patellar / quadriceps tendon rupture or patella fracture. A surgical problem.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What is a “locked knee” and what causes it?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: A springy block to full extension — classically a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear mechanically obstructing the joint.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: Which tests assess the cruciate and collateral ligaments?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: ACL: Lachman / anterior drawer / pivot shift. PCL: posterior drawer / sag sign. Collaterals: valgus (MCL) and varus (LCL) stress.
Joint-line tenderness, McMurray’s test, Thessaly test and Apley grind — supported by a history of twisting, locking and delayed swelling.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What must you always do with an atraumatic hot swollen knee?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Aspirate it — send for Gram stain / culture (septic) and polarised-light microscopy (crystals). Never assume gout without excluding sepsis.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: Which crystal arthropathy commonly affects the knee, and its X-ray clue?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Pseudogout (CPPD) commonly affects the knee; the X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis (calcification of cartilage).

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What causes anterior knee pain in a young adult, worse on stairs and prolonged sitting?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Patellofemoral pain syndrome — a clinical diagnosis, managed with physiotherapy and quadriceps / VMO strengthening.
Traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents — pain and a tender bony lump over the tuberosity, worse with activity; self-limiting.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: What is the significance of posterior knee pain / fullness with calf swelling?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: A Baker’s cyst; a ruptured Baker’s cyst mimics a DVT — do a Doppler ultrasound to exclude the clot.

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: When should a knee be X-rayed after trauma?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Apply the Ottawa knee rules: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, tenderness at the fibular head, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to weight-bear (4 steps).

signs__MSK__Knee Pain.front: Why must you examine the hip when assessing a child’s knee pain?
signs__MSK__Knee Pain.back: Hip pathology (Perthes, SUFE) commonly refers pain to the knee — a child with knee pain and a normal knee may have a hip problem.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What clinical cluster should make you diagnose giant cell arteritis?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Age >50 with a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a tender / thickened / pulseless temporal artery and raised ESR / CRP — often with polymyalgia rheumatica overlap.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What is jaw claudication and why is it important?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Aching in the jaw / masseter that builds up during chewing and eases on stopping — it reflects masseter ischaemia and is the most specific symptom of GCA (and marks high risk of visual loss).

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What is the feared complication of giant cell arteritis?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Sudden, irreversible visual loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION) — and if untreated the fellow eye can be lost within days.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What visual symptoms warn of impending blindness in GCA?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular visual loss), transient blurring, or diplopia (extra-ocular muscle ischaemia). These demand emergency treatment.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What is the immediate management of suspected GCA?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Start high-dose corticosteroids at once — before the biopsy. IV methylprednisolone if there are any visual symptoms; otherwise oral prednisolone 40–60 mg/day. Add aspirin, a PPI and bone protection.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: Does starting steroids invalidate the temporal artery biopsy?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: No — the biopsy remains informative if taken within 1–2 weeks of starting steroids. Never delay treatment to obtain the biopsy.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What are the key investigations in GCA?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: ESR / CRP / plasma viscosity (ESR often >50) and FBC; temporal artery biopsy (long segment — beware skip lesions) and/or temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign); large-vessel imaging (CT/PET/MRA) if aortitis is suspected.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: Why can a temporal artery biopsy be falsely negative?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: GCA affects the artery in a patchy distribution (skip lesions), so a short or unaffected segment may miss it — take a long segment, and a negative biopsy does not exclude the diagnosis.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What is the relationship between GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: They overlap — up to ~half of GCA patients have PMR (shoulder- and hip-girdle pain and morning stiffness), and a proportion of PMR patients develop GCA. Both respond dramatically to steroids (PMR at lower doses).

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What are the fundoscopy findings of GCA-related optic neuropathy?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: A pale, swollen optic disc (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) with a relative afferent pupillary defect on the affected side.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What are the main mimics of the jaw-claudication / scalp-tenderness cluster?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction or dental disease (pain at the joint/tooth, clicking); herpes zoster of the scalp (dermatomal vesicles); trigeminal neuralgia; tension-type headache.

signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.front: What long-term vascular complication can GCA cause?
signs__MSK__Jaw Claudication & Scalp Ten.back: Large-vessel involvement can lead to aortic aneurysm and dissection, plus limb claudication and bruits — warranting long-term monitoring.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: What is the classic clinical picture of a fractured neck of femur?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: An older patient who has fallen, cannot weight-bear, with the leg shortened and externally rotated and pain on any hip movement or axial loading.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: Why is the leg shortened and externally rotated in a NOF fracture?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: The proximal fragment is pulled up and outward by the iliopsoas and short external rotators, producing shortening and external rotation.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: Why does the intracapsular vs extracapsular distinction matter?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: An intracapsular fracture can disrupt the femoral-head blood supply → risk of avascular necrosis / non-union, so displaced ones are replaced; extracapsular fractures spare the blood supply and are fixed.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: How is a displaced intracapsular NOF fracture managed surgically?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Replacement: total hip replacement in fitter, more active patients, or hemiarthroplasty in less mobile patients.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: How are extracapsular NOF fractures managed?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Fixation: a dynamic hip screw for intertrochanteric fractures, or an intramedullary nail for subtrochanteric / reverse-oblique patterns.
A grading (I–IV) of intracapsular femoral neck fracture displacement that helps guide the replace-vs-fix decision (higher grades = more displaced = replace).

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: A patient has hip pain and cannot weight-bear after a fall, but the X-ray is normal. What should you do?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Do not discharge — suspect an occult fracture and proceed to MRI (or CT / bone scan).

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: How does a posterior hip dislocation differ from a NOF fracture on inspection?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: A posterior hip dislocation gives a shortened, INTERNALLY rotated and adducted leg (vs the externally rotated leg of a fracture).

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: What non-orthopaedic priorities are essential in a hip-fracture patient?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Early analgesia (consider a fascia iliaca block), resuscitation, correcting anaemia / dehydration / AKI, finding the cause of the fall, and an orthogeriatric pathway.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: What is the target time to surgery for a hip fracture and why?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Within 36 hours — delay increases morbidity and mortality in these frail patients.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: What underlying bone problem underlies most hip fractures, and what follow-up is needed?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: Most are fragility (osteoporotic) fractures — arrange a bone-health and falls assessment and osteoporosis treatment.

signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.front: What is fat embolism syndrome in the context of a proximal femoral fracture?
signs__MSK__Shortened & Externally Rotat.back: A complication (typically 24–72h after long-bone / femoral fracture) of confusion, hypoxia (respiratory distress) and a petechial rash from marrow fat entering the circulation.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Radicular leg pain — sharp, shooting, often electric pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal distribution from compression of a lumbosacral nerve root (usually L5 or S1), commonly with paraesthesia ± weakness.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What is the commonest cause of sciatica?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: A prolapsed intervertebral disc compressing a nerve root. Other causes: lateral / foraminal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and (rarely) tumour or infection.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: How do you distinguish radicular from referred (somatic) leg pain?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Radicular: below the knee, dermatomal, shooting, with positive nerve-tension tests (SLR). Referred somatic: dull, above the knee, non-dermatomal, tension tests negative.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What is the must-not-miss emergency to screen for in every sciatica?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Cauda equina syndrome — bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder / bowel dysfunction, reduced anal tone, sexual dysfunction → emergency whole-spine MRI and surgical decompression.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What are the signs of an L5 radiculopathy?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Pain / numbness over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot / big toe, weak dorsiflexion and big-toe extension (foot drop), and no reflex change.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What are the signs of an S1 radiculopathy?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Pain / numbness over the posterior leg, sole and lateral foot, weak plantar flexion, and a lost ankle jerk.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What are the signs of an L4 radiculopathy?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Pain over the anterior thigh / medial shin, weak knee extension, a reduced knee jerk, and a positive femoral stretch test.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: Which examination tests are used for nerve-root tension in sciatica?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Straight-leg raise (and the highly specific crossed SLR) for L5 / S1 roots, and the femoral stretch test for L3 / L4 roots.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: When should sciatica be imaged with MRI?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Not routinely early. Image if there are red flags (cauda equina, malignancy, infection), a progressive / severe neurological deficit, or persistent pain (>6–12 weeks) in a potential surgical candidate.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: What is the initial management of uncomplicated sciatica?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Conservative: analgesia (including neuropathic agents), staying active, and physiotherapy — most cases settle within 6–12 weeks. Reserve epidural injection or discectomy for persistent / severe radiculopathy.

signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.front: Which features suggest a serious (non-disc) cause of sciatica?
signs__MSK__Sciatica (Radicular Leg Pain.back: Night pain, weight loss or cancer history (malignant root compression); fever, IV drug use or immunosuppression (discitis / epidural abscess); a progressive motor deficit such as a new foot drop.

Neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis — leg pain on walking, eased by flexion), hip osteoarthritis / trochanteric pain (groin / lateral, negative SLR), peripheral neuropathy, vascular claudication and piriformis syndrome.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What is the pivotal question when a neuropathic (diabetic) patient presents with a hot swollen foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Is it acute Charcot neuroarthropathy or infection (cellulitis / osteomyelitis / septic arthritis)? They look alike but management diverges (offload vs antibiotics ± surgery) and both are limb-threatening.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What are the features of an acute Charcot foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: A hot, red, swollen foot, typically >2°C warmer than the other, with little pain despite the inflammation, often after minor trauma, intact skin and bounding pulses; systemically well.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What features favour infection over Charcot in a hot swollen foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: A portal of entry (ulcer / skin break), systemic upset (fever, raised WCC / CRP), erythema that persists on elevation, and an ulcer that probes to bone (osteomyelitis).

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What is the elevation test in the hot neuropathic foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Elevate the leg for a few minutes: erythema that fades favours Charcot (dependent hyperaemia), whereas erythema that persists favours infection.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: Why can the X-ray be misleading in acute Charcot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: The X-ray is often normal early; the earliest changes (marrow oedema) are seen only on MRI. A normal X-ray does not exclude Charcot — treat on clinical suspicion.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What is the immediate management of a suspected acute Charcot foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Offload immediately (total-contact cast), keep non-weight-bearing, and refer to the diabetic-foot MDT the same day — delay leads to bony collapse and a rocker-bottom deformity.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What deformity results from a missed acute Charcot foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: A rocker-bottom foot (midfoot collapse), which ulcerates and can lead to amputation.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: How is osteomyelitis suggested and confirmed in the diabetic foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Suggested by an ulcer that probes to bone, chronicity and raised inflammatory markers; confirmed with MRI and bone biopsy / culture.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: Which single imaging test best distinguishes Charcot from osteomyelitis?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: MRI — it shows Charcot marrow oedema and bony fragmentation versus the ulcer-to-bone tracking and cortical destruction of osteomyelitis.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What is the significance of pulses in the hot neuropathic foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: A neuropathic foot is warm and well-perfused with bounding pulses; a pulseless hot foot is neuroischaemic — a different, higher-risk problem needing vascular assessment.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: Which other diagnoses cause a hot swollen foot and should be considered?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Gout (acute first-MTP pain, podagra), DVT (unilateral calf swelling), fracture / sprain (pain blunted by neuropathy), and necrotising fasciitis.

signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.front: What are the warning features of necrotising fasciitis in the foot?
signs__MSK__Hot Swollen Neuropathic Foot.back: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky rapidly-spreading skin and systemic collapse — a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What does the Simmonds (Thompson) test assess?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: A complete Achilles tendon rupture. With the patient prone and feet over the edge, squeezing the calf normally plantarflexes the foot; if the tendon is ruptured the foot does not move (positive).

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: How is the Simmonds / Thompson test performed?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Position the patient prone with the feet hanging over the end of the couch (or kneeling on a chair), then squeeze the calf (gastrocnemius–soleus) and watch for plantarflexion of the foot.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What is a positive Simmonds test?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Absent plantarflexion of the foot when the calf is squeezed — the divided Achilles tendon cannot transmit the squeeze. It indicates a complete rupture.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: Why can active plantarflexion be preserved despite a complete Achilles rupture?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Other muscles (tibialis posterior, the toe flexors, peronei) can produce weak plantarflexion, so a patient may still move the foot — preserved active movement does not exclude a rupture.
With the patient prone, flex both knees to 90°: the ruptured side falls into neutral or dorsiflexion while the intact side rests in plantarflexion (loss of resting Achilles tone).

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: Where is the palpable gap usually felt in an Achilles rupture?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: About 2–6 cm above the calcaneal insertion, in the relatively avascular watershed zone of the tendon.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What is the classic mechanism and patient for an Achilles rupture?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: A sudden pop or feeling of being “kicked” in the back of the leg during push-off, typically in a middle-aged recreational athlete playing racquet / court sports.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: Which drugs are associated with Achilles tendon rupture?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin) and corticosteroids; gout and chronic tendinopathy also predispose.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: How is an Achilles rupture usually diagnosed?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Clinically — a positive Simmonds test, a palpable gap and a positive Matles test. Ultrasound or MRI is reserved for uncertain or partial tears.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What condition can mimic an Achilles rupture with calf pain but a negative squeeze test?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: A medial gastrocnemius tear (“tennis leg”) — and a DVT must also be excluded (Doppler ultrasound if the calf is swollen and tender).

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What sign at rest suggests a ruptured Achilles tendon?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Increased resting dorsiflexion of the foot on the affected side, from loss of the tendon’s resting tone.

signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.front: What are the broad management options for an Achilles rupture?
signs__MSK__Simmonds / Thompson Test (Ac.back: Conservative (immobilisation in an equinus cast / functional boot with graded rehab) or surgical repair — decided with orthopaedics based on patient factors.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: De Quervain’s tenosynovitis — a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist (the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons at the radial styloid).
The patient tucks the thumb into the palm and makes a fist over it (or the examiner grasps the thumb); the wrist is then ulnar-deviated. Sharp pain over the radial styloid is a positive test.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: Which tendons are involved in De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: The abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB), which run together through the first dorsal compartment over the radial styloid.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: What is the difference between the Finkelstein and Eichhoff tests?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: The Eichhoff test is the common fist-clench variant (thumb inside a clenched fist, then ulnar deviation). The true Finkelstein has the examiner grasp the thumb and pull it into ulnar deviation. They are often used interchangeably.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: Which patients classically develop De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: New mothers (“mummy thumb”) from repeatedly lifting the baby, people with repetitive thumb / wrist use (texting, gaming, occupational strain), and those with rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: How is De Quervain’s tenosynovitis distinguished from first carpometacarpal (CMC) osteoarthritis?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: De Quervain’s causes tendon pain over the radial styloid (positive Finkelstein). 1st CMC OA causes pain at the thumb-base joint, a positive grind test and squaring of the thumb base.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: What important fracture must be excluded in radial-sided wrist pain after trauma?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: A scaphoid fracture — suggested by anatomical-snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand; X-ray (with repeat or MRI if initially normal).

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: Where exactly is the pain and tenderness in De Quervain’s?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: Over the radial styloid, a centimetre or two proximal to the thumb base, along the APL / EPB tendons — often with local swelling and pain on thumb use / gripping.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: What is the initial (conservative) management of De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
What are the escalation options if De Quervain’s does not settle with conservative treatment?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: A corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal compartment, and surgical release of the compartment if refractory.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: What is Wartenberg’s syndrome and how does it differ from De Quervain’s?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: Compression of the superficial radial (sensory) nerve, causing dorsoradial tingling / numbness rather than the tendon pain of De Quervain’s; Finkelstein’s may be uncomfortable but the problem is sensory.

signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.front: How is De Quervain’s tenosynovitis usually diagnosed?
signs__MSK__Finkelstein's Test (De Querv.back: Clinically — a positive Finkelstein test with radial-styloid tenderness; ultrasound can confirm tendon-sheath thickening / effusion if needed.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: The hip abductor mechanism — gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve, L4–S1) — which keeps the pelvis level when standing on one leg.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: How is Trendelenburg's test performed and what is a positive result?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: Ask the patient to stand on one leg. Normal: the opposite (lifted) side of the pelvis stays level or rises. Positive: the pelvis drops on the lifted (non-stance) side.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: On which side does the pelvis drop relative to the affected hip?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: On the side opposite the affected hip — the mnemonic is “sound side sags”. The abnormal hip is the one being stood on.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: Which muscles and nerve are responsible for a positive Trendelenburg sign?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: Weakness or mechanical failure of the gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1).

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: What are the four broad categories of cause for a positive Trendelenburg sign?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: Nerve (superior gluteal nerve palsy, L5 radiculopathy), muscle (proximal myopathy / dystrophy), joint / pain (hip OA, fracture — abductor inhibition), and abnormal fulcrum (DDH, coxa vara, AVN, prosthesis).

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: What gait results from hip abductor weakness?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: A Trendelenburg gait — the trunk lurches over the weak (weight-bearing) hip; if bilateral, a waddling gait.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: How can hip surgery or an intramuscular injection cause a positive Trendelenburg sign?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: By damaging the superior gluteal nerve (e.g. surgical approach) or injuring the gluteal muscles / nerve with a misplaced IM injection, weakening the abductors.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: Why can a painful hip give a positive Trendelenburg sign without true muscle weakness?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: Pain causes reflex inhibition of the abductors (e.g. in hip OA or fracture), producing a positive sign even when the muscles are structurally intact.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: What is a delayed Trendelenburg sign?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: The pelvis stays level initially but drops after several seconds of single-leg stance — it still counts as a positive test, so observe for ~30 seconds.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: Which paediatric hip conditions can produce a positive Trendelenburg sign?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), Perthes disease and the sequelae of SUFE — by altering the femoral head / abductor lever arm.

signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).front: How do you localise the cause once Trendelenburg is positive?
signs__MSK__Trendelenburg's Sign (Hip).back: A painless drop after hip surgery suggests a nerve cause; a bilateral waddle suggests myopathy; a painful hip with reduced rotation suggests OA; a child’s limp suggests a structural hip disorder.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: A child climbing up their own body to stand from the floor — they turn prone, push into a “bear” position and “walk” their hands up their thighs to lever themselves upright, because of proximal weakness.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: Which muscle groups are weak when Gower's sign is positive?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: The pelvic-girdle muscles — the hip extensors (gluteus maximus) and knee extensors (quadriceps), i.e. proximal lower-limb weakness.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: Which condition classically causes Gower's sign in a young boy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: Duchenne muscular dystrophy — though the sign occurs in any proximal myopathy and is not specific.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What is the single most useful first investigation when Gower’s sign is seen?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: A creatine kinase (CK) — it is markedly raised in muscular dystrophy.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What are the key clinical features of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: A boy aged 3–5 with delayed walking, a waddling gait, frequent falls, calf pseudohypertrophy, positive Gower’s sign and a very high CK.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What is the inheritance and molecular basis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: X-linked recessive, from mutations in the dystrophin gene (absent dystrophin).

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: How is Duchenne muscular dystrophy confirmed?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: A markedly raised CK followed by genetic testing for the dystrophin mutation, with muscle biopsy reserved for uncertain cases.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What is the difference between Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: Both are dystrophinopathies, but Becker has reduced (not absent) dystrophin, so it is milder with later onset and slower progression.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What surveillance is essential in muscular dystrophy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: Cardiac (dilated cardiomyopathy) and respiratory monitoring, within a multidisciplinary team, plus genetic counselling for the family.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: Besides muscular dystrophy, what other causes produce a positive Gower’s sign?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: Spinal muscular atrophy, inflammatory myopathy (juvenile dermatomyositis), congenital and metabolic myopathies, and, in adults, any proximal myopathy.

signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.front: What treatment slows decline in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
signs__MSK__Gower's Sign (Proximal Weakn.back: Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone or deflazacort), alongside MDT care, physiotherapy and cardiac / respiratory management.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: What does the painful arc test assess?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Subacromial impingement — pain through the mid-arc (~60–120°) of abduction as the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa are compressed under the acromion.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: How is the painful arc elicited and what is a positive result?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Ask the patient to actively abduct the arm through full range. Positive = pain appearing in the 60–120° mid-arc that eases below and above it.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: What structures are compressed during a positive painful arc?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: The supraspinatus tendon and the subacromial bursa, pinched between the greater tuberosity and the acromion / coraco-acromial arch.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: What does a high painful arc (above ~160°) suggest instead?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Acromioclavicular joint pathology — supported by focal ACJ tenderness and a positive scarf (cross-body adduction) test.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: Which other tests confirm subacromial impingement?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: The Neer test (passive forward flexion) and the Hawkins–Kennedy test (arm flexed to 90°, then internally rotated).

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: How do you tell impingement from a rotator cuff tear when the arc is painful?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: A cuff tear adds weakness and a positive drop-arm test, with preserved passive range; simple impingement has pain but relatively preserved strength.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: Which conditions produce a positive painful arc?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Rotator-cuff tendinopathy, subacromial bursitis and calcific tendinitis — all forms of subacromial impingement.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: How is subacromial impingement usually managed?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Relative rest and physiotherapy, NSAIDs, and a subacromial corticosteroid injection; subacromial decompression if refractory.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: What global shoulder finding argues against a simple painful arc?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: Loss of both active AND passive movement (especially external rotation) — this indicates a capsular problem (frozen shoulder or glenohumeral OA), not impingement.

signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.front: Is the painful arc specific for impingement?
signs__MSK__Painful Arc (Subacromial Imp.back: It is sensitive but not specific — interpret it alongside the arc height, the impingement tests and cuff-strength testing.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: What does the empty-can (Jobe) test assess?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: The supraspinatus muscle/tendon — the most commonly injured rotator-cuff tendon. A positive test indicates supraspinatus tendinopathy or a tear.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: How is the empty-can test performed?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: The arm is held at 90° abduction in the scapular plane (~30° forward) with the thumb pointing down (as if emptying a can); the examiner presses down against the patient’s resistance.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: What is a positive empty-can test?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: Pain and / or weakness on resisted downward pressure, compared with the other side.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: How do you distinguish tendinopathy from a tear using the empty-can test?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: Pain with reasonable strength suggests tendinopathy / impingement; marked weakness (especially with a positive drop-arm) suggests a full-thickness supraspinatus tear.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: What is the full-can variant and when is it used?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: The same test with the thumb pointing up; it loads the supraspinatus more comfortably and is used when the empty-can position is too painful.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: Which other tests complete the rotator-cuff examination?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: The painful arc and Neer / Hawkins–Kennedy (impingement), resisted external rotation (infraspinatus) and the lift-off test (subscapularis).

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: How is a suspected supraspinatus (cuff) tear confirmed?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: With ultrasound or MRI of the shoulder, which confirms and sizes the tear.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: Why does a full-thickness supraspinatus tear cause a positive drop-arm test?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: The torn supraspinatus can no longer hold the abducted arm, so when the patient tries to lower it slowly (or it is released), the arm drops.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: What finding suggests a frozen shoulder rather than a cuff tear when the empty-can test is weak?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: Loss of passive as well as active movement (a capsular pattern, external rotation worst) — a cuff tear preserves passive range.

signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.front: How is supraspinatus tendinopathy / impingement usually managed?
signs__MSK__Empty-can Test (Jobe / Supra.back: Physiotherapy, NSAIDs and a subacromial corticosteroid injection; significant tears may need surgical cuff repair.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which feature best indicates that joint pain is INFLAMMATORY rather than mechanical?
options: Early-morning stiffness lasting over 30-60 minutes that eases with use
Pain that progressively worsens through the day with continued use
Relief of pain only with complete rest
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Prolonged morning stiffness (>30–60 min) that eases with use is the hallmark of inflammatory joint pain.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: A patient presents with a single acutely hot, swollen, painful knee. What is the essential first step?
options: Arrange an outpatient MRI scan in about six weeks
Aspirate the joint before giving antibiotics
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: A single hot joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate (Gram/culture/crystals) before antibiotics.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: How many joints are involved in an 'oligoarthritis'?
A symmetrical polyarthritis of the MCP and PIP joints with an hour of morning stiffness suggests which diagnosis?
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness is typical of rheumatoid arthritis.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which distribution and history are most typical of osteoarthritis?
options: MCPs and wrists with long morning stiffness
DIP and weight-bearing joints, worse with use
1st MTP joint with sudden night-time pain
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: OA favours the DIP and weight-bearing joints and is worse with use, with bony swelling.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Sudden severe pain, redness and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint overnight is most likely:
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Acute podagra (1st MTP) is the classic presentation of gout.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which examination finding is characteristic of an ARTICULAR (rather than periarticular) problem?
options: Pain on movement in all planes with an effusion
Pain only on one specific resisted movement
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Articular pathology gives pain on all planes of movement, often with an effusion.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: An asymmetrical large-joint arthritis with dactylitis and a scaly rash suggests which group of conditions?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis of the small joints
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Asymmetrical large-joint arthritis with dactylitis and psoriasis points to a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Arthritis that moves from one joint to another over days ('migratory') is characteristic of which cause?
options: Gonococcal or rheumatic fever / Lyme arthritis
Mechanical degenerative joint pain from chronic overuse
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Migratory arthritis suggests gonococcal, rheumatic fever, viral or Lyme disease.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Widespread pain with multiple tender points, fatigue and NORMAL inflammatory markers suggests:
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Widespread pain with tender points and normal CRP/ESR and no synovitis suggests fibromyalgia.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which investigation is mandatory for any acutely hot, swollen joint?
options: Joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals
An outpatient ultrasound scan in around six weeks
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Joint aspiration (Gram/culture/crystals) is mandatory to exclude sepsis in a hot joint.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: A patient with likely gout has a single hot joint. Why should you still aspirate it?
options: Septic arthritis can coexist with gout
Gout never affects a single joint
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: Sepsis can coexist with crystal arthritis, so a hot joint is always aspirated even when gout is likely.

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which set of features accompanying arthralgia should raise concern for connective tissue disease?
options: Brief joint stiffness that is rapidly relieved by rest
Bony swelling of the DIP joints
Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers and Raynaud's
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: A photosensitive rash, oral ulcers and Raynaud’s point to a connective tissue disease (e.g. SLE).

signs__MSK__Joint Pain.question: Which best describes the correct order of a joint examination?
Which of the following is a first-line blood test panel for undifferentiated inflammatory joint pain?
options: CRP/ESR, urate, RF, anti-CCP and ANA
signs__MSK__Joint Pain.explanation: First-line rheumatology screening includes CRP/ESR, urate, RF, anti-CCP and ANA.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.question: What is the single most important initial step for an acute hot swollen joint?
options: Reassurance and routine outpatient clinic follow-up
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.explanation: A hot joint is septic until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics for Gram/culture/crystals.

signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.question: Which organism is the commonest cause of septic arthritis?
signs__MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint.explanation: Staph aureus is the commonest cause of septic arthritis.
